questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Insertional inactivation of a selectable marker in pBR322
questions.question: Foreign DNA is ligated into the PstI site of the plasmid pBR322. This site lies inside the ampicillin-resistance gene; the tetracycline-resistance gene is left intact. After transformation, Escherichia coli cells are spread on a plate containing tetracycline, and the colonies are then replica-plated onto a plate containing ampicillin. Colony 1 grows on both plates. Colony 2 grows on the tetracycline plate but not on the ampicillin plate. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) Colony 1 carries the recombinant plasmid, because a cell with an insert must show both resistances
B) Colony 2 is an untransformed cell, because it has lost ampicillin resistance
C) Colony 2 carries the recombinant plasmid; the insert has inactivated the ampicillin-resistance gene, while the intact tetracycline-resistance gene on the same plasmid lets it grow on tetracycline
D) Neither colony can be recombinant, because an insert in pBR322 inactivates both resistance genes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Colony 2 carries the recombinant plasmid; the insert has inactivated the ampicillin-resistance gene, while the intact tetracycline-resistance gene on the same plasmid lets it grow on tetracycline.
Concept: A selectable marker lets transformants be picked out. When foreign DNA is inserted inside one antibiotic-resistance gene of a vector, that gene is inactivated (insertional inactivation). Recombinants then lose that one resistance but keep the other.
Why: Every colony on the first plate has a plasmid, because untransformed E. coli is sensitive to tetracycline. Colony 1 is still resistant to ampicillin, so its ampicillin-resistance gene is intact: it carries the plasmid without an insert. Colony 2 has lost ampicillin resistance, which happens when the PstI site inside that gene holds the foreign DNA. So colony 2 is the recombinant.
Why not the others: (A) Keeping both resistances shows the PstI site is not interrupted, so colony 1 is non-recombinant. (B) An untransformed cell would not grow on the tetracycline plate at all. (D) The PstI site lies only inside the ampicillin-resistance gene; the tetracycline-resistance gene is untouched.
Key point: The marker that is interrupted is lost; the marker that is intact selects transformants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Bt toxin: why the protoxin harms the insect but not the bacterium or a mammal
questions.question: Bacillus thuringiensis makes a Cry protein that kills bollworm larvae feeding on Bt cotton, yet the bacterium itself is not harmed, and the protein does not harm mammals that eat the cotton seed. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) The protein is made as an inactive protoxin; it becomes active only in the alkaline gut of the insect, where it binds to the midgut epithelial cells and makes pores that cause them to swell and burst
B) The protein is active inside the bacterium, but the bacterium makes a second protein that neutralises it
C) The protein is activated by the acidic stomach of the insect and is destroyed in the alkaline gut of mammals
D) The protein forms a double-stranded RNA that silences an essential mRNA of the insect only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The protein is made as an inactive protoxin; it becomes active only in the alkaline gut of the insect, where it binds to the midgut epithelial cells and makes pores that cause them to swell and burst.
Concept: Some strains of Bacillus thuringiensis form protein crystals that contain an inactive toxin (protoxin), coded by cry genes. When an insect eats them, the alkaline pH of its gut dissolves the crystals and converts the protoxin into the active toxin. The active toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells and creates pores, so the cells swell and lyse, and the insect dies.
Why: Inside the bacterium the protein stays as an inactive protoxin, so it does no harm there. Activation needs the alkaline conditions of the insect gut. The stomach of a mammal is acidic, so the protoxin is not activated there.
Why not the others: (B) No second neutralising protein is needed; the toxin is simply inactive until it reaches the insect gut. (C) It reverses the conditions: activation needs an alkaline pH, which is found in the insect gut, while the mammalian stomach is acidic. (D) Silencing of mRNA by double-stranded RNA is RNA interference, used against nematodes; the Cry protein is a protein toxin, not RNA.
Key point: Bt protoxin → activated by alkaline insect gut → pores in midgut cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading carrying capacity and the point of fastest growth from a logistic curve
questions.question: The figure shows the number of yeast cells per microlitre in a flask of nutrient medium, counted every 2 hours for 20 hours. No medium was added during the experiment. Which statement is supported by the graph?
options: A) The carrying capacity is about 300 cells per microlitre, because the curve is steepest there
B) The rate of increase dN/dt is greatest at the start, when the population is smallest
C) The curve is J-shaped, so resources were not limiting at any time
D) The carrying capacity is about 600 cells per microlitre, and the rate of increase is greatest when the population is near half of this value
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The carrying capacity is about 600 cells per microlitre, and the rate of increase is greatest when the population is near half of this value.
Concept: With limited resources a population shows logistic (sigmoid) growth: \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=rN\left(\dfrac{K-N}{K}\right)\). The curve has a lag phase, a phase of fast growth, and then levels off at the carrying capacity K.
Why: From the figure, the curve levels off at 600 cells per microlitre from about 16 hours onwards, so K is about 600. The slope of the curve (dN/dt) is greatest at about 8 hours, where N is about 300, which is K/2. This agrees with the logistic equation, where rN(K − N)/K is largest at N = K/2.
Why not the others: (A) 300 is where growth is fastest; the carrying capacity is the level at which the curve flattens. (B) At the start the curve is almost flat, so dN/dt is small even though the per-cell rate is high. (C) The curve flattens at the top, so it is S-shaped, not J-shaped; resources became limiting.
Key point: Logistic curve: flattens at K, steepest at K/2.
questions.image_alt: Graph of yeast cell density against time from 0 to 20 hours; the curve starts near 20, rises in an S shape and levels off at 600 cells per microlitre.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Biological concept of species: reproductive isolation of look-alike populations
questions.question: Two populations of frogs, P and Q, live in the same pond and look identical in every external feature. In the laboratory, a P × Q cross gives hybrid tadpoles that grow into adults, but these adults never produce offspring. In the pond, P breeds in March and Q breeds in July. How should P and Q be classified?
options: A) As one species, because members of a species are grouped by their external appearance
B) As two species, because they do not interbreed to give fertile offspring, even though they look alike
C) As one species, because a cross between them does produce offspring
D) As two genera, because their hybrids are sterile
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) As two species, because they do not interbreed to give fertile offspring, even though they look alike.
Concept: A species is a group of individuals with fundamental similarities that can interbreed in nature and give fertile offspring. Reproductive isolation separates one species from another.
Why: P and Q are isolated in two ways. In nature they breed in different months, so they do not meet as mates. Even when forced to cross, the hybrids are sterile. They therefore form two separate gene pools, which makes them two species even though they look the same.
Why not the others: (A) Appearance alone is not enough; look-alike populations can be separate species. (C) Offspring must be fertile; sterile hybrids do not join the two gene pools. (D) Sterile hybrids show separate species, not separate genera; a genus is a group of related species.
Key point: The test of a species is fertile interbreeding, not appearance.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Lateral movement of membrane proteins and membrane fluidity
questions.question: A human cell and a mouse cell are fused. The membrane proteins of the human cell carry a red label and those of the mouse cell a green label. At 37 °C the two colours are evenly mixed over the whole fused cell within 40 minutes. When the same fusion is kept at 15 °C, the colours stay on separate halves for a long time. No new proteins are made during the experiment. Which explanation fits both results?
options: A) Membrane proteins move sideways within the lipid bilayer, and this movement depends on the fluidity of the lipids, which falls at low temperature
B) New labelled proteins are made at 37 °C and inserted all over the membrane
C) Proteins flip quickly from the inner to the outer face of the membrane at 37 °C
D) The membrane is a fixed layer of lipid between two layers of protein, so proteins move only when heated
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Membrane proteins move sideways within the lipid bilayer, and this movement depends on the fluidity of the lipids, which falls at low temperature.
Concept: In the fluid mosaic model, the quasi-fluid lipid bilayer allows proteins to move laterally within it. This fluidity is important for cell growth, cell division, secretion and the formation of intercellular junctions.
Why: The colours mix because labelled proteins drift sideways through the bilayer. At 15 °C the lipids are less fluid, so the drift is very slow and the two halves stay separate. Since no new proteins are made, the mixing must be movement of existing proteins.
Why not the others: (B) The question states that no new proteins are made. (C) Flipping from one face to the other does not spread the label around the cell, and it is very rare for proteins. (D) A rigid protein–lipid–protein sandwich is the older model; it cannot explain mixing at 37 °C, which is not heating above body temperature.
Key point: Mixing of labelled proteins is direct evidence that the bilayer is fluid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Identifying carbohydrates and lipids from hydrolysis products and simple tests
questions.question:
Four biomolecules were tested. The results are shown below.

Compound | Products of complete hydrolysis | Other observation
P | glucose only | turns blue-black with iodine
Q | glucose and fructose | none
R | glycerol and three fatty acids | none
S | glycerol, two fatty acids, phosphate and choline | none

Which identification is correct?
options: A) P cellulose, Q sucrose, R lecithin, S triglyceride
B) P starch, Q maltose, R triglyceride, S lecithin
C) P starch, Q sucrose, R triglyceride, S lecithin
D) P starch, Q sucrose, R lecithin, S triglyceride
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) P starch, Q sucrose, R triglyceride, S lecithin.
Concept: Starch forms helices that hold iodine and give a blue-black colour; cellulose does not. Sucrose is made of glucose and fructose; maltose is two glucose units. A triglyceride is glycerol esterified with three fatty acids. A phospholipid such as lecithin has glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphorylated group (choline in lecithin).
Why: P gives only glucose and stains blue-black, so it is starch. Q gives glucose and fructose, so it is sucrose. R is glycerol with three fatty acids, a triglyceride. S contains phosphate and choline, so it is lecithin.
Why not the others: (A) Cellulose does not give a blue-black colour with iodine, and R and S are swapped. (B) Maltose gives only glucose on hydrolysis, not glucose and fructose. (D) R and S are swapped: the compound with phosphate and choline is lecithin.
Key point: Phosphate + choline = lecithin; three fatty acids = triglyceride; glucose + fructose = sucrose.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing photosystem I and photosystem II: reaction centres and their roles
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares photosystem I (PS I) and photosystem II (PS II) in the light reaction of green plants?
options: A) PS I has the reaction centre P680 and is linked with the splitting of water, while PS II has P700

B) The reaction centre of PS II absorbs best at 680 nm and its electron loss is made good by splitting of water; the reaction centre of PS I absorbs best at 700 nm and its electrons finally reduce NADP⁺
C) Both photosystems have the same reaction centre, chlorophyll b, and differ only in their position in the thylakoid
D) PS II passes its excited electrons directly to NADP⁺, while PS I passes them back to water
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The reaction centre of PS II absorbs best at 680 nm and its electron loss is made good by splitting of water; the reaction centre of PS I absorbs best at 700 nm and its electrons finally reduce NADP⁺.
Concept: Each photosystem has a light-harvesting complex of pigments around a reaction centre of chlorophyll a. In PS I the reaction centre has an absorption peak at 700 nm (P700); in PS II it has a peak at 680 nm (P680). In the Z scheme, PS II acts first and PS I second.
Why: When P680 loses electrons, it gets them back from the splitting of water, which releases oxygen. The electrons travel through the electron transport chain to PS I. Excited electrons from P700 pass through another chain and finally reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH.
Why not the others: (A) It swaps the reaction centres: P680 belongs to PS II, which is the one linked with water splitting. (C) The reaction centre of both photosystems is chlorophyll a, not chlorophyll b, and they differ in their absorption peaks. (D) Electrons go from water to PS II, from PS II to PS I, and from PS I to NADP⁺; nothing goes back to water.
Key point: PS II = P680, water splitting; PS I = P700, NADP⁺ reduction.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Seed dormancy and germination: effect of a mutant unable to make abscisic acid
questions.question: A mutant maize plant cannot make abscisic acid (ABA). Its seeds develop normally on the cob, but many of them begin to germinate while still attached to the parent plant. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) The mutant makes extra ABA in the seed, which speeds up germination
B) The mutant cannot make gibberellin, so the seed coat does not form
C) The seeds lack a seed coat, so water enters before they are shed
D) ABA normally keeps the maturing seed dormant; without it the seed starts to germinate as soon as conditions allow
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ABA normally keeps the maturing seed dormant; without it the seed starts to germinate as soon as conditions allow.
Concept: Abscisic acid plays an important part in seed development, maturation and dormancy. By inducing dormancy, ABA helps seeds withstand desiccation and delays germination until conditions are suitable. Gibberellins work the other way and promote germination.
Why: In the mutant there is no ABA to hold the seed in a dormant state. The embryo is therefore free to grow while the seed is still moist on the parent plant, so it germinates early.
Why not the others: (A) The mutant cannot make ABA at all, and ABA delays germination rather than speeding it. (B) Gibberellins promote germination; lack of gibberellin would delay it, and the question says the seeds develop normally. (C) The seeds develop normally; the defect is hormonal, not a missing seed coat.
Key point: ABA = dormancy; gibberellin = germination.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Expiratory reserve volume and functional residual capacity worked back from spirometer capacities
questions.question: A spirometer record of a healthy adult gives a vital capacity of 4000 mL and an inspiratory capacity of 3000 mL. The residual volume, found by a separate method, is 1200 mL. What are the expiratory reserve volume and the functional residual capacity?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1000 mL and 2200 mL.
Concept: Inspiratory capacity (IC) = TV + IRV. Vital capacity (VC) = TV + IRV + ERV = IC + ERV. Functional residual capacity (FRC) = ERV + RV is the air left in the lungs after a normal expiration. The residual volume cannot be breathed out, so a simple spirometer cannot measure RV or FRC directly.
Given: VC = 4000 mL, IC = 3000 mL, RV = 1200 mL.
Formula/Principle: ERV = VC − IC; FRC = ERV + RV.
Step 1: ERV = 4000 − 3000 = 1000 mL.
Step 2: FRC = 1000 + 1200 = 2200 mL.
Why: The vital capacity is the inspiratory capacity plus the extra air that can be forced out after a normal expiration, which is the ERV. Adding the residual volume to the ERV gives the FRC. Check: total lung capacity = VC + RV = 5200 mL = IC + FRC = 3000 + 2200 mL.
Why not the others: (B) 4200 mL adds the inspiratory capacity to the residual volume; FRC uses the ERV, not the IC. (C) It adds VC and IC instead of subtracting, which counts TV and IRV twice. (D) 1500 mL adds a tidal volume of 500 mL to the ERV instead of the residual volume.
Key point: VC = IC + ERV; FRC = ERV + RV; TLC = IC + FRC.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Order of events in blood coagulation
questions.question:
The four events below take place when blood clots at a cut.
1. Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin.
2. Injured tissue and platelets release factors that form thrombokinase.
3. Prothrombin is converted to thrombin.
4. Threads of fibrin trap blood cells and form the clot.
Which is the correct order?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2, 3, 1, 4.
Concept: Coagulation is a cascade. An injury releases factors from tissue and platelets that start the cascade and give the enzyme thrombokinase. Thrombokinase converts inactive prothrombin into thrombin, and thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads. Calcium ions are needed for the process.
Why: Each step makes the enzyme for the next one: injury → thrombokinase (2) → thrombin (3) → fibrin (1) → network of fibrin trapping formed elements (4).
Why not the others: (A) Thrombin cannot form before thrombokinase, which is the enzyme that makes it. (B) Fibrin cannot form before thrombin, the enzyme that converts fibrinogen. (D) Fibrinogen is converted only after the injury has started the cascade.
Key point: Thrombokinase → thrombin → fibrin → clot.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Ammonotelism and ureotelism during frog metamorphosis
questions.question: The main nitrogenous waste of frogs was measured at two stages. A tadpole living fully in water excreted mostly ammonia. The adult frog, which spends much time on land, excreted mostly urea. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) Tadpoles have no kidneys, so they cannot make urea
B) Adult frogs are uricotelic, so urea is only a minor waste in them
C) Ammonia is less toxic than urea, so the adult that lives on land excretes ammonia
D) Ammonia is highly toxic and needs much water to be removed, which suits an aquatic larva; urea is less toxic and can be held in the body, which suits an animal that spends time on land
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Ammonia is highly toxic and needs much water to be removed, which suits an aquatic larva; urea is less toxic and can be held in the body, which suits an animal that spends time on land.
Concept: Animals are ammonotelic, ureotelic or uricotelic depending on their main nitrogenous waste. Ammonia is the most toxic and needs large amounts of water for its removal, so it suits aquatic animals. Urea is less toxic; it is made in the liver and can be stored for some time before it is removed.
Why: The change from ammonia to urea matches the change from a fully aquatic tadpole to an adult that lives partly on land, where water must be saved. Adult amphibians are ureotelic.
Why not the others: (A) The tadpole does excrete; the choice of ammonia is because of its watery habitat. (B) The measurement shows urea as the main waste; uricotelic animals excrete mainly uric acid. (C) Ammonia is more toxic than urea, not less.
Key point: Less water available → less toxic waste: ammonia → urea → uric acid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Diabetes insipidus: source of vasopressin in the hypothalamus–neurohypophysis system
questions.question: After a head injury, a patient passes about 10 litres of very dilute urine a day and is always thirsty. There is no glucose in the urine and the blood glucose is normal. The cause is a lack of one hormone. Which hormone is it, and where is it made?
options: A) Antidiuretic hormone, made by cells of the posterior pituitary
B) Antidiuretic hormone, made by neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary
C) Insulin, made by the beta cells of the pancreas
D) Aldosterone, made by the adrenal cortex
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Antidiuretic hormone, made by neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.
Concept: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) increases reabsorption of water in the distal parts of the nephron. It is made by the hypothalamus, carried along nerve axons to the neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary), stored there and released. A lack of ADH causes diabetes insipidus: large volumes of dilute urine and thirst.
Why: The urine is dilute and plentiful, but there is no glucose, so the problem is water reabsorption, not sugar. That points to ADH. The neurohypophysis only stores and releases ADH; the hormone is synthesised in the hypothalamus.
Why not the others: (A) The posterior pituitary does not make ADH; it stores and releases hormone made in the hypothalamus. (C) Lack of insulin causes diabetes mellitus, with glucose in the urine and high blood glucose. (D) Aldosterone acts mainly on sodium reabsorption; its lack does not give 10 litres of very dilute urine with normal glucose.
Key point: ADH and oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus and released from the neurohypophysis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting pollen grains, meiotic divisions and male gametes from microspore mother cells
questions.question: An anther has 4 microsporangia, and each microsporangium contains 50 microspore mother cells. Every microspore mother cell completes meiosis, every microspore develops into a pollen grain, and every pollen grain later forms its male gametes. How many male gametes are formed in all, and how many meiotic divisions took place?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1600 male gametes; 200 meiotic divisions.
Concept: Each microspore mother cell undergoes one meiosis to give a tetrad of four microspores. Each microspore becomes a pollen grain. The generative cell of the pollen grain divides mitotically to give two male gametes.
Given: 4 microsporangia × 50 microspore mother cells; 1 meiosis per mother cell; 2 male gametes per pollen grain.
Formula/Principle: meioses = mother cells; pollen grains = 4 × meioses; male gametes = 2 × pollen grains.
Step 1: Mother cells = 4 × 50 = 200, so 200 meiotic divisions.
Step 2: Pollen grains = 200 × 4 = 800; male gametes = 800 × 2 = 1600.
Why: Number of microspore mother cells = 4 × 50 = 200, so there are 200 meiotic divisions. Pollen grains = 200 × 4 = 800. Male gametes = 800 × 2 = 1600.
Why not the others: (A) 800 is the number of pollen grains; each pollen grain gives two male gametes. (B) It counts one meiosis for each pollen grain; one meiosis gives four microspores. (D) It counts only the cells of one microsporangium as meioses and forgets the division of the generative cell.
Key point: 1 meiosis → 4 pollen grains → 8 male gametes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Path of sperms through the male duct system
questions.question: Which sequence shows the correct path of sperms from their place of formation to the ejaculatory duct?
options: A) Seminiferous tubule → rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct
B) Rete testis → seminiferous tubule → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct
C) Seminiferous tubule → rete testis → epididymis → vasa efferentia → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct
D) Seminiferous tubule → vasa efferentia → rete testis → vas deferens → epididymis → ejaculatory duct
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Seminiferous tubule → rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct.
Concept: Sperms are formed in the seminiferous tubules of the testis. The male sex accessory ducts are the rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis and vas deferens. The seminiferous tubules open into the vasa efferentia through the rete testis; the vasa efferentia leave the testis and open into the epididymis on its posterior surface.
Why: Following the ducts outwards: seminiferous tubules → rete testis (network inside the testis) → vasa efferentia (leave the testis) → epididymis (stores sperms) → vas deferens (ascends into the abdomen) → joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct.
Why not the others: (B) Sperms are formed in the seminiferous tubules, so the path starts there, not at the rete testis. (C) The vasa efferentia lie before the epididymis, not after it. (D) The rete testis comes before the vasa efferentia, and the epididymis comes before the vas deferens.
Key point: Tubules → rete → efferentia → epididymis → deferens → ejaculatory duct.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Phenotypic classes in a dihybrid cross with incomplete dominance and co-dominance
questions.question: In a plant, flower colour shows incomplete dominance (RR red, Rr pink, rr white). A seed protein shows co-dominance: allele S¹ makes form 1, allele S² makes form 2, and the heterozygote S¹S² makes both forms. The two genes assort independently. Two plants that are pink and make both seed proteins are crossed. How many phenotypic classes appear among the offspring, and what fraction of the offspring has the same phenotype as the parents?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 9 classes; 1/4.
Concept: With complete dominance a monohybrid cross gives two phenotypes (3 : 1). With incomplete dominance or with co-dominance the heterozygote has its own phenotype, so the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio, 1 : 2 : 1, and there are three phenotypes.
Given: both parents Rr S¹S²; the genes assort independently; each heterozygote has its own phenotype.
Formula/Principle: classes for two independent genes = (classes for gene 1) × (classes for gene 2); probabilities multiply.
Step 1: Rr × Rr → RR : Rr : rr = 1 : 2 : 1 (red, pink, white); S¹S² × S¹S² → 1 : 2 : 1 (form 1, both, form 2).
Step 2: Classes = 3 × 3 = 9; P(pink and both proteins) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Why: The parents are Rr S¹S². Each gene alone gives 3 phenotypes in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1. For two independent genes the classes multiply: 3 × 3 = 9 phenotypic classes. The parental phenotype (pink, both proteins) needs Rr (probability 1/2) and S¹S² (probability 1/2), so its fraction is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Why not the others: (A) 4 classes in 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 assume complete dominance for both genes. (B) 1/16 is the fraction of one homozygous class such as RR S¹S¹, not of the double heterozygote. (C) 6 classes would need one gene with complete dominance; here neither gene has it.
Key point: In incomplete dominance and co-dominance, phenotype ratio = genotype ratio (1 : 2 : 1).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Multiple alleles of the ABO blood group: parents' genotypes from a child's blood group
questions.question: A man of blood group A and a woman of blood group B have a child of blood group O. What are the genotypes of the parents, and what is the probability that their next child has blood group AB?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(I^Ai\) and \(I^Bi\); probability 1/4.
Concept: The ABO blood group is controlled by three alleles, \(I^A\), \(I^B\) and i. \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) are co-dominant with each other, and both are dominant over i. Blood group O is ii.
Why: The O child is ii, so each parent must carry i. The father is therefore \(I^Ai\) and the mother \(I^Bi\). An AB child needs \(I^A\) from the father (1/2) and \(I^B\) from the mother (1/2): 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Why not the others: (A) Homozygous parents could not give an O child. (C) 1/2 multiplies only one parent's probability. (D) A father \(I^AI^A\) has no i allele, so an ii child would be impossible.
Key point: An O child means both parents carry i.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Positive charge of histones and the formation of nucleosomes
questions.question: In a mutant, most lysine and arginine residues of the core histone proteins are replaced by glutamate, which is negatively charged. What is the most likely effect on the packaging of DNA in the nucleus?
options: A) DNA wraps more tightly around the histones, because glutamate is a larger residue
B) There is no effect, because DNA is held to histones by hydrogen bonds between the bases
C) Chromatin becomes more condensed heterochromatin, because the negative histones attract non-histone chromosomal proteins instead of DNA
D) Nucleosomes fail to form and chromatin is less compact, because the negatively charged DNA is now repelled by the histones
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Nucleosomes fail to form and chromatin is less compact, because the negatively charged DNA is now repelled by the histones.
Concept: Histones are rich in the basic residues lysine and arginine, which carry positive charges in their side chains. They form a positively charged histone octamer. The negatively charged DNA is wrapped around this octamer to form a nucleosome, the repeating unit of chromatin, which is further coiled to give the chromatin fibre.
Why: The binding of DNA to histones depends on attraction between the negative phosphate groups of DNA and the positive histone side chains. Replacing positive residues with negative glutamate turns this attraction into repulsion, so DNA cannot wrap around the octamer and the first level of packaging fails.
Why not the others: (A) Removing positive charges weakens the binding; size does not make it tighter. (B) DNA binds histones by ionic attraction to the phosphate backbone, not by hydrogen bonds between bases, which hold the two DNA strands together. (C) Heterochromatin forms by packing DNA on nucleosomes; without nucleosomes, chromatin becomes less condensed, not more.
Key point: Positive histone octamer + negative DNA phosphate backbone = nucleosome.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Homologous and analogous organs: divergent and convergent evolution
questions.question: Which set contains only pairs that show convergent evolution?
options: A) Eye of the octopus and eye of a mammal; flipper of a penguin and flipper of a dolphin; sweet potato and potato
B) Thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita; eye of the octopus and eye of a mammal; sweet potato and potato
C) Forelimb of a whale and forelimb of a bat; flipper of a penguin and flipper of a dolphin; heart of a frog and heart of a bird
D) Thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita; forelimb of a whale and forelimb of a bat; heart of a frog and heart of a bird
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Eye of the octopus and eye of a mammal; flipper of a penguin and flipper of a dolphin; sweet potato and potato.
Concept: Analogous structures do the same job but have different origins; they result from convergent evolution. Homologous structures have the same origin but may do different jobs; they result from divergent evolution.
Why: The eyes of the octopus and the mammal, the flippers of the penguin and the dolphin, and the sweet potato (a modified root) and the potato (a modified stem) are all analogous: similar function, different origin. So every pair in A is convergent.
Why not the others: (B) The thorn of Bougainvillea and the tendril of Cucurbita are both modified stems (axillary buds), so they are homologous. (C) The forelimbs of a whale and a bat, and the hearts of vertebrates, are homologous. (D) All three pairs are homologous, which shows divergent evolution.
Key point: Same job, different origin = analogous (convergent); same origin = homologous (divergent).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Industrial melanism as directional selection: change in the frequency of a phenotype
questions.question: In a woodland, a sample of 1000 peppered moths taken before industrialisation had 900 light and 100 dark moths. After soot had darkened the tree trunks for many years, a sample of 1000 had 150 light and 850 dark moths. What type of natural selection does this show, and what is the percentage of dark moths in the later sample?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Directional selection; 85%.
Concept: Natural selection can be stabilising (the mean is favoured), directional (one extreme is favoured, so the mean shifts) or disruptive (both extremes are favoured). In industrial England, dark moths on dark trunks escaped predators, so their proportion rose.
Given: before, 900 light and 100 dark out of 1000; after, 150 light and 850 dark out of 1000.
Formula/Principle: percentage = (number of dark moths ÷ sample size) × 100.
Step 1: Dark moths rose from 10% to 85%, a shift towards one extreme.
Step 2: 850 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 85%.
Why: The population shifted from mostly light to mostly dark, which is a shift towards one extreme: directional selection. Dark moths in the later sample = 850 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 85%.
Why not the others: (A) Stabilising selection keeps the common type; here the common type was replaced. (B) Disruptive selection favours both extremes, and 15% is the share of light moths. (D) The type is right, but 15% is the share of light moths, not dark ones.
Key point: One extreme favoured, mean shifts = directional selection.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Erythrocytic cycle of Plasmodium: growth in the number of infected red blood cells and timing of fever
questions.question: In a malaria patient, assume that the cycle of Plasmodium in red blood cells takes 48 hours, that each infected cell bursts to release 16 merozoites, and that every merozoite infects a new red blood cell. A fever spike occurs each time infected cells burst. At the first spike, 1000 infected cells burst. How many red blood cells are infected just after the third spike, and how long after the first spike does the third spike occur?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(4.1\times10^6\); 96 hours.
Concept: Sporozoites from the mosquito multiply first in liver cells and then in red blood cells. When infected red blood cells burst, they release merozoites and the toxic haemozoin, which causes the chill and high fever that recur in cycles.
Given: cycle = 48 h; 16 merozoites per burst cell; 1000 cells burst at the first spike.
Formula/Principle: newly infected cells after the k-th spike = 1000 × 16^k; time from spike 1 to spike k = (k − 1) × 48 h.
Step 1: After spike 3: 1000 × 16³ = 4 096 000 ≈ 4.1 × 10⁶.
Step 2: Time = (3 − 1) × 48 = 96 h.
Why: First spike: 1000 cells burst, giving 1000 × 16 = 16 000 newly infected cells. Second spike (48 h): 16 000 × 16 = 256 000 newly infected cells. Third spike (96 h): 256 000 × 16 = 4 096 000 ≈ \(4.1\times10^6\) newly infected cells. The third spike comes two cycles after the first: 2 × 48 = 96 hours.
Why not the others: (A) \(2.6\times10^5\) is the number just after the second spike. (C) The number is right, but three spikes span two intervals, not three. (D) It adds 16 000 three times instead of multiplying by 16 at each cycle.
Key point: Merozoite numbers multiply each cycle; n spikes span n − 1 cycles.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols: slow step and ease of dehydration
questions.question: Ethanol, propan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol are each heated with concentrated sulfuric acid to give alkenes. Which step of the mechanism is the slowest (rate-determining), and which of the three alcohols is dehydrated most easily?
options: A) Protonation of the OH group; ethanol
B) Loss of water from the protonated alcohol to give a carbocation; 2-methylpropan-2-ol
C) Loss of a proton from the carbocation; 2-methylpropan-2-ol
D) Loss of water from the protonated alcohol to give a carbocation; ethanol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Loss of water from the protonated alcohol to give a carbocation; 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
Concept: Acid-catalysed dehydration takes place in three steps: (1) fast protonation of the OH group, (2) slow loss of water to form a carbocation, (3) fast loss of a proton from the carbon next to the positive carbon to give the alkene. The ease of dehydration is 3° > 2° > 1°, because it follows the stability of the carbocation formed in the slow step.
Why: The slow step is the formation of the carbocation. 2-Methylpropan-2-ol gives the tertiary carbocation \(\ce{(CH3)3C+}\), which is stabilised by three alkyl groups, so it forms fastest. Ethanol would have to give a primary carbocation, which is least stable.
Why not the others: (A) Protonation of an oxygen lone pair by a strong acid is fast, and ethanol is the slowest of the three. (C) Loss of a proton from a carbocation is fast. (D) The step is right, but ethanol forms the least stable carbocation and is dehydrated least easily (it needs about 443 K).
Key point: Rate of dehydration follows carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1°.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reactivity of aldehydes and ketones towards nucleophilic addition
questions.question: Arrange the following in decreasing order of reactivity towards addition of HCN: \(\ce{HCHO}\), \(\ce{CH3CHO}\), \(\ce{CH3COCH3}\), \(\ce{C6H5COCH3}\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\ce{HCHO > CH3CHO > CH3COCH3 > C6H5COCH3}\).
Concept: In nucleophilic addition the nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon. The reaction is faster when the carbonyl carbon is more positive (electronic effect) and when it is less crowded (steric effect). Alkyl groups release electrons and add bulk; a phenyl group adds bulk and reduces the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon by resonance.
Why: HCHO has no alkyl group and is the most reactive. \(\ce{CH3CHO}\) has one methyl group. \(\ce{CH3COCH3}\) has two, so it is less reactive than any of the aldehydes here. In \(\ce{C6H5COCH3}\) the phenyl ring is conjugated with the C=O group and is bulky, so it is the least reactive.
Why not the others: (A) It places a ketone above two aldehydes, which reverses both the electronic and the steric effects. (B) Acetophenone is less reactive than acetone because of resonance with the ring and its larger group. (C) This is the increasing order, not the decreasing one.
Key point: More alkyl or aryl groups on C=O → less positive, more crowded carbon → slower nucleophilic addition.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Drawback of the Rutherford model: stability of an orbiting electron
questions.question: Rutherford's nuclear model replaced Thomson's model of the atom. Which observation could the Rutherford model not explain, and why?
options: A) The stability of the atom: an electron moving in a circular orbit is accelerating, so by electromagnetic theory it should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus
B) The deflection of a few α-particles through large angles, because the positive charge is spread through the whole atom
C) The passage of most α-particles straight through a gold foil, because the atom is mostly empty space
D) The electrical neutrality of the atom, because the nucleus has no charge
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The stability of the atom: an electron moving in a circular orbit is accelerating, so by electromagnetic theory it should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus.
Concept: Thomson pictured the atom as a uniform sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it. Rutherford's α-scattering experiment showed a tiny, dense, positive nucleus, with electrons moving around it. The Rutherford model could not explain why the atom is stable, nor the line spectrum of hydrogen.
Why: An electron in a circular orbit changes its direction of motion all the time, so it is accelerating. Classical electromagnetic theory says an accelerated charge radiates energy. The orbit would then shrink and the electron would fall into the nucleus, which does not happen.
Why not the others: (B) Large-angle deflection is what the Rutherford model explains well; a positive charge spread through the whole atom is Thomson's picture. (C) The model explains this too: most of the atom is empty. (D) The nucleus is positive, and the electrons outside balance its charge, so neutrality is explained.
Key point: Rutherford model: explains scattering, fails on atomic stability and line spectra.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Radius of an atom compared with its cations of different charge
questions.question: Arrange Fe, \(\ce{Fe^2+}\) and \(\ce{Fe^3+}\) in decreasing order of radius, and give the reason.
options: A) \(\ce{Fe^3+ > Fe^2+ > Fe}\), because a higher positive charge makes the ion swell
B) \(\ce{Fe^2+ > Fe > Fe^3+}\), because a 2+ ion has the most stable configuration
C) \(\ce{Fe > Fe^2+ > Fe^3+}\), because the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons more tightly as electrons are removed
D) \(\ce{Fe > Fe^3+ > Fe^2+}\), because \(\ce{Fe^3+}\) has a half-filled 3d subshell, which is larger
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\ce{Fe > Fe^2+ > Fe^3+}\), because the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons more tightly as electrons are removed.
Concept: A cation is smaller than its parent atom. It has fewer electrons while the nuclear charge stays the same, so the effective nuclear charge felt by each remaining electron is larger and the electron cloud is pulled in. The more electrons removed, the smaller the ion.
Why: Fe has 26 electrons, \(\ce{Fe^2+}\) has 24 and \(\ce{Fe^3+}\) has 23, all with 26 protons. Fe also loses its 4s electrons on forming \(\ce{Fe^2+}\), so the outermost shell changes. Removing a further 3d electron in \(\ce{Fe^3+}\) increases the attraction on each remaining electron again, so \(\ce{Fe^3+}\) is the smallest.
Why not the others: (A) This is the increasing order; a higher positive charge contracts the ion. (B) Stability of a configuration does not make an ion larger than its neutral atom. (D) The half-filled 3d subshell makes \(\ce{Fe^3+}\) stable, but it still has fewer electrons than \(\ce{Fe^2+}\) and is smaller.
Key point: For one element: atom > lower cation > higher cation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Formal charges in the Lewis structure of ozone and the observed equal bond lengths
questions.question: One Lewis structure of ozone is O=O–O, in which the central oxygen atom has one lone pair, the terminal oxygen joined by the double bond has two lone pairs, and the terminal oxygen joined by the single bond has three lone pairs. Experiment shows that both O–O bonds in ozone have the same length, 128 pm. What are the formal charges on the double-bonded terminal O, the central O and the single-bonded terminal O, in that order?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0, +1, −1.
Concept: Formal charge = (valence electrons of the free atom) − (non-bonding electrons) − ½(bonding electrons). When one Lewis structure cannot represent a molecule, resonance between equivalent structures is used.
Why: Double-bonded terminal O: 6 − 4 − ½(4) = 0. Central O: 6 − 2 − ½(6) = +1. Single-bonded terminal O: 6 − 6 − ½(2) = −1. The sum is 0, as it must be for a neutral molecule. The equal bond lengths (128 pm, between the O–O single bond of 148 pm and the O=O double bond of 121 pm) show that the two equivalent resonance structures contribute equally.
Why not the others: (B) The central O has only 5 electrons assigned to it (2 + 3), one fewer than its 6 valence electrons, so its formal charge cannot be 0. (C) The double-bonded terminal O has 6 assigned electrons, so it is 0, not +1. (D) It reverses the signs: the central O has fewer assigned electrons than its valence count, so it is positive.
Key point: Formal charge = V − N − B/2; equal bond lengths in O₃ are explained by resonance.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Relation between bond order, bond length and bond enthalpy for carbon–carbon bonds
questions.question:
The table gives carbon–carbon bond lengths and bond enthalpies.

Bond | Bond length / pm | Bond enthalpy / kJ mol⁻¹
C–C (ethane) | 154 | 348
C=C (ethene) | 134 | 614
C≡C (ethyne) | 120 | 839
C–C (benzene) | 139 | —

Which conclusion is supported by the data?
options: A) Bond enthalpy decreases as the bond order increases
B) The carbon–carbon bonds in benzene have a bond order between 1 and 2
C) Each π bond adds more energy than the σ bond does, since the C≡C enthalpy is more than three times the C–C enthalpy
D) The longest of the three bonds is the strongest
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The carbon–carbon bonds in benzene have a bond order between 1 and 2.
Concept: As the bond order increases, the bond length decreases and the bond enthalpy increases. In resonance-stabilised molecules, the bonds that resonance makes equal have intermediate bond orders and lengths.
Why: The order of C–C bond lengths is single (154) > double (134) > triple (120). The benzene bond (139 pm) lies between the single and the double bond, so its bond order lies between 1 and 2 (it is 1.5, since the two Kekulé structures contribute equally).
Why not the others: (A) The enthalpies rise from 348 to 614 to 839 kJ mol⁻¹ as the bond order rises. (C) Three times 348 is 1044 kJ mol⁻¹, which is more than 839; each π bond adds less than a σ bond (614 − 348 = 266 kJ mol⁻¹). (D) The longest bond, C–C at 154 pm, has the lowest enthalpy.
Key point: Higher bond order → shorter and stronger bond; benzene C–C lies between single and double.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Work in each step and heat for a complete cycle of an ideal gas read from a P–V diagram
questions.question: The figure shows a cycle A → B → C → A for 1 mol of an ideal gas on a pressure–volume diagram. Step A → B is at constant volume, step B → C is the straight line shown, and step C → A is at constant pressure. Use 1 L bar = 100 J and the sign convention in which w is the work done on the gas. What are the work done on the gas in step C → A and the heat absorbed by the gas in the complete cycle?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(w_{CA}=+2000\ \mathrm J;\ q_{\text{cycle}}=+2000\ \mathrm J\).
Concept: First law: \(\Delta U=q+w\). For a complete cycle \(\Delta U=0\), so \(q_{\text{cycle}}=-w_{\text{cycle}}\). Work done on a gas is \(w=-\int p\,dV\); on a P–V diagram, the magnitude of the work in a step is the area under that step, and the net work for a cycle is the area enclosed.
Why: From the figure, A = (10 L, 1 bar), B = (10 L, 3 bar), C = (30 L, 1 bar). In C → A the gas is compressed at 1 bar from 30 L to 10 L: \(w_{CA}=-(1)(10-30)=+20\ \mathrm{L\,bar}=+2000\ \mathrm J\). In A → B the volume is constant, so \(w_{AB}=0\). In B → C the gas expands; the area under the line is a trapezium with average pressure 2 bar over 20 L: \(w_{BC}=-(2)(20)=-40\ \mathrm{L\,bar}=-4000\ \mathrm J\). Net \(w=0-4000+2000=-2000\ \mathrm J\), so \(q_{\text{cycle}}=+2000\ \mathrm J\). Check: the enclosed triangle has area \(\tfrac12(20\ \mathrm L)(2\ \mathrm{bar})=20\ \mathrm{L\,bar}=2000\ \mathrm J\), and the cycle runs clockwise, so the gas does net work and absorbs net heat.
Why not the others: (A) A compression has work done on the gas, so \(w_{CA}\) is positive, not negative. (B) It takes the sign of q from the work; the gas does net work in a clockwise cycle and must absorb the same amount of heat. (C) Only \(\Delta U\) is zero for a cycle; q and w are path functions and need not be zero.
Key point: Cycle: \(\Delta U=0\), \(q=-w\), and |w| = enclosed area; clockwise on P–V means net heat absorbed.
