questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Heat, work and internal energy change when an ideal gas is heated at constant pressure
questions.question: 2.00 mol of a monatomic ideal gas is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 350 K. For this gas \(C_{V,m}=\tfrac32R\) and \(C_{p,m}=C_{V,m}+R\). Take R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and the sign convention in which w is the work done on the gas. What are q, ΔU and w?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) q = 2079 J, ΔU = 1247 J, w = −831 J.
Concept: At constant pressure the heat absorbed equals the enthalpy change, \(q_p=\Delta H=nC_{p,m}\Delta T\). For an ideal gas, ΔU depends only on temperature, \(\Delta U=nC_{V,m}\Delta T\), whatever the path. The first law \(\Delta U=q+w\) links them, and for an ideal gas \(C_p-C_V=R\).
Given: \(n=2.00\ \mathrm{mol},\ \Delta T=50\ \mathrm K,\ C_{V,m}=\tfrac32R=12.47\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}mol^{-1}},\ C_{p,m}=\tfrac52R=20.79\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}mol^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(q_p=nC_{p,m}\Delta T;\ \Delta U=nC_{V,m}\Delta T;\ w=\Delta U-q=-nR\Delta T\)
Step 1: \(q_p=2.00\times20.79\times50=2079\ \mathrm J\).
Step 2: \(\Delta U=2.00\times12.47\times50=1247\ \mathrm J\).
Step 3: \(w=1247-2079=-831\ \mathrm J\); check: \(-nR\Delta T=-2.00\times8.314\times50=-831\ \mathrm J\).
Why: Part of the heat raises the internal energy, and the rest is used by the gas to push back the surroundings as it expands. Work done by the gas means negative w in this convention.
Why not the others: (A) ΔU = q only at constant volume; here the gas expands and does work. (B) It swaps \(C_p\) and \(C_V\) and gives the wrong sign to w. (D) The gas expands, so work is done by it and w is negative.
Key point: Constant pressure: \(q=nC_p\Delta T\), \(\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T\), \(w=-nR\Delta T\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Degree of dissociation of PCl5 from vapour density; effect of an inert gas at constant pressure
questions.question: \(\ce{PCl5(g) <=> PCl3(g) + Cl2(g)}\). At a certain temperature the vapour density of the equilibrium mixture is 62.0. (P = 31.0, Cl = 35.5.) What is the degree of dissociation of \(\ce{PCl5}\), and what happens to it if argon is added at constant total pressure and temperature?
options: B) About 0.68; it does not change, because argon does not take part in the reaction
D) About 0.68; it decreases, because the total number of moles increases
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) About 0.68; it increases.
Concept: When one molecule dissociates into two, the number of moles rises from 1 to (1 + α), so the vapour density falls in the same ratio: \(\dfrac{D}{d}=1+\alpha\), where D is the vapour density with no dissociation and d the observed value. Adding an inert gas at constant pressure increases the volume and lowers the partial pressures of the reacting gases, so the equilibrium shifts to the side with more moles of gas.
Given: \(M(\ce{PCl5})=31.0+5\times35.5=208.5;\ d=62.0\)
Formula/Principle: \(D=\dfrac M2;\ \alpha=\dfrac{D-d}{d}\)
Step 1: \(D=\dfrac{208.5}{2}=104.25\).
Step 2: \(\alpha=\dfrac{104.25-62.0}{62.0}=\dfrac{42.25}{62.0}=0.68\).
Why: At constant pressure the added argon spreads the reacting gases over a larger volume. The reaction quotient \(\dfrac{p_{\ce{PCl3}}p_{\ce{Cl2}}}{p_{\ce{PCl5}}}\) falls below K, because two partial pressures are multiplied on top and only one is below. The reaction moves forward, so α increases.
Why not the others: (B) An inert gas has no effect at constant volume, but at constant pressure it lowers the partial pressures and shifts the equilibrium. (C) 0.41 divides by D instead of d: \(\tfrac{42.25}{104.25}\). (D) The total number of moles includes argon, but only the moles of the reacting gases decide the direction; the shift is towards more moles of gas.
Key point: \(\alpha=\dfrac{D-d}{d}\) for A ⇌ B + C; inert gas at constant pressure favours the side with more gas moles.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Counting structural isomers of C5H11Cl and those with a chiral carbon
questions.question: How many structural isomers have the formula \(\ce{C5H11Cl}\), and how many of these structural isomers have a chiral carbon atom?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 8 and 3.
Concept: Structural isomers of a monochloroalkane come from the different carbon skeletons and the different positions of Cl on each. A carbon atom bonded to four different groups is chiral and gives optical isomers.
Given: \(\ce{C5H11Cl}\); carbon skeletons of \(\ce{C5H12}\): pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane.
Formula/Principle: count the distinct positions for Cl on each skeleton; then look for a carbon with four different groups.
Step 1: Pentane: 1-, 2- and 3-chloropentane (3).
Step 2: 2-Methylbutane: 1-chloro-2-methylbutane, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, 2-chloro-3-methylbutane, 1-chloro-3-methylbutane (4).
Step 3: 2,2-Dimethylpropane: 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane (1). Total = 3 + 4 + 1 = 8.
Step 4: Chiral: 2-chloropentane (C-2: H, Cl, \(\ce{CH3}\), \(\ce{C3H7}\)); 1-chloro-2-methylbutane (C-2: H, \(\ce{CH3}\), \(\ce{C2H5}\), \(\ce{CH2Cl}\)); 2-chloro-3-methylbutane (C-2: H, Cl, \(\ce{CH3}\), \(\ce{CH(CH3)2}\)). So 3.
Why: The others have no carbon with four different groups: 3-chloropentane has two ethyl groups on C-3; 2-chloro-2-methylbutane has two methyl groups on C-2; 1-chloro-3-methylbutane and the neopentyl chloride have no such carbon.
Why not the others: (A) It misses 1-chloro-2-methylbutane, whose chiral C-2 does not carry the chlorine. (B) It leaves out 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane, from the third skeleton. (C) It counts only the straight-chain isomers.
Key point: \(\ce{C5H11Cl}\): 3 + 4 + 1 = 8 structural isomers; 3 of them are chiral.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Wurtz reaction with two different alkyl halides and Kolbe electrolysis
questions.question: A mixture of bromomethane and bromoethane is treated with sodium in dry ether. Which alkanes are formed? Which one of these could also be made by Kolbe electrolysis of aqueous sodium propanoate?
options: B) Methane, ethane and propane; ethane
C) Ethane, propane and butane; butane
D) Ethane, propane and butane; hexane
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ethane, propane and butane; butane.
Concept: In the Wurtz reaction, two alkyl groups from alkyl halides join: \(\ce{2R-X + 2Na -> R-R + 2NaX}\). With two different halides, every pairing of the alkyl groups is possible. In Kolbe electrolysis, the carboxylate ion loses \(\ce{CO2}\) at the anode and two alkyl radicals join: \(\ce{2RCOO- -> R-R + 2CO2 + 2e-}\).
Why: Methyl + methyl gives ethane; methyl + ethyl gives propane; ethyl + ethyl gives butane. Sodium propanoate \(\ce{CH3CH2COONa}\) gives the ethyl radical, and two ethyl radicals give butane, \(\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH3}\).
Why not the others: (A) Two different halides do not react only with each other; all three pairings occur. (B) The Wurtz reaction always joins two alkyl groups, so it cannot give methane, and Kolbe electrolysis of propanoate does not give ethane. (D) The carboxyl carbon is lost as \(\ce{CO2}\), so propanoate gives an ethyl radical and butane, not hexane.
Key point: Mixed Wurtz → all R–R pairings; Kolbe of RCOO⁻ → R–R with loss of CO₂.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Boiling and melting points of cis- and trans-but-2-ene
questions.question: Compare cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene. Which isomer has the higher boiling point, and which has the higher melting point?
options: A) trans has both the higher boiling point and the higher melting point
B) cis has the higher boiling point; trans has the higher melting point
C) cis has both the higher boiling point and the higher melting point
D) trans has the higher boiling point; cis has the higher melting point
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) cis has the higher boiling point; trans has the higher melting point.
Concept: In cis-but-2-ene both methyl groups are on the same side of the double bond, so the small bond dipoles add and the molecule is polar. In the trans isomer the dipoles cancel and the molecule is non-polar. Boiling point depends on intermolecular attraction; melting point also depends on how well the molecules pack in the solid.
Why: The polar cis isomer has dipole–dipole attraction, so it boils higher (about 277 K) than trans (about 274 K). The trans isomer is more symmetrical and packs better in the crystal, so it melts higher (about 168 K) than cis (about 134 K).
Why not the others: (A) The non-polar trans isomer boils lower. (C) The cis isomer packs less well, so it melts lower. (D) It reverses both effects.
Key point: cis-alkene: polar, higher bp; trans-alkene: symmetrical, higher mp.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Henry's law constants: order of gas solubility and mole fraction of dissolved oxygen
questions.question: Henry's law constants \(K_H\) in water at 298 K are: He 145 kbar, \(\ce{N2}\) 76.5 kbar, \(\ce{O2}\) 34.9 kbar and \(\ce{CO2}\) 1.67 kbar. What is the order of solubility of these gases at the same partial pressure, and what is the mole fraction of oxygen dissolved in water when the partial pressure of oxygen is 0.20 bar?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\ce{CO2}\) > \(\ce{O2}\) > \(\ce{N2}\) > He; \(5.7\times10^{-6}\).
Concept: Henry's law: \(p=K_Hx\), where x is the mole fraction of the gas in the solution. At a given partial pressure, a higher \(K_H\) means a lower solubility.
Given: \(K_H(\ce{O2})=34.9\ \mathrm{kbar}=3.49\times10^4\ \mathrm{bar};\ p=0.20\ \mathrm{bar}\)
Formula/Principle: \(x=\dfrac{p}{K_H}\)
Step 1: Order of \(K_H\): He > \(\ce{N2}\) > \(\ce{O2}\) > \(\ce{CO2}\), so the order of solubility is the reverse: \(\ce{CO2}\) > \(\ce{O2}\) > \(\ce{N2}\) > He.
Step 2: \(x=\dfrac{0.20}{3.49\times10^4}=5.7\times10^{-6}\).
Why: \(\ce{CO2}\) has by far the smallest \(K_H\) and is the most soluble; helium has the largest and is the least soluble.
Why not the others: (A) It orders the gases by \(K_H\), which is the reverse of solubility. (B) It multiplies p by \(K_H\) instead of dividing. (C) It leaves \(K_H\) in kbar, which makes x a thousand times too large.
Key point: Larger \(K_H\) = less soluble; \(x=p/K_H\) with consistent pressure units.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: EMF of a copper concentration cell from the Nernst equation and the electrode that gains mass
questions.question: Two copper electrodes dip into copper(II) sulfate solutions of concentration 0.010 M and 1.0 M, joined by a salt bridge. The cell is at 298 K, and 2.303RT/F = 0.059 V. A high-resistance voltmeter is connected and then a small current is allowed to flow. What does the voltmeter read, and which electrode gains mass?
options: A) 0.059 V; the electrode in the 1.0 M solution
B) 0.059 V; the electrode in the 0.010 M solution
C) 0.118 V; the electrode in the 1.0 M solution
D) 0 V, because both electrodes are made of copper
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.059 V; the electrode in the 1.0 M solution.
Concept: A concentration cell has the same electrode in two solutions of different concentration. Its standard EMF is zero, but the Nernst equation gives a non-zero EMF: \(E=\dfrac{0.059}{n}\log\dfrac{c_{\text{cathode}}}{c_{\text{anode}}}\). The cathode is the electrode in the more concentrated solution.
Why: \(E=\dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{1.0}{0.010}=\dfrac{0.059}{2}\times2=0.059\ \mathrm V\). Reduction \(\ce{Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu}\) takes place in the 1.0 M solution, so copper is deposited and that electrode gains mass. The electrode in the 0.010 M solution dissolves, raising its concentration, until the two become equal.
Why not the others: (B) Copper dissolves from the electrode in the dilute solution; it is the anode and loses mass. (C) It uses n = 1; two electrons are transferred for each copper ion. (D) \(E^\circ=0\), but the EMF depends on concentrations and is not zero here.
Key point: Concentration cell: \(E=\dfrac{0.059}{n}\log\dfrac{c_2}{c_1}\); the concentrated side is the cathode.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Finding the rate law and rate constant from initial-rate data
questions.question:
For the reaction \(\ce{A + 2B -> products}\), the following initial rates were measured at a fixed temperature.

Experiment | [A] / mol L⁻¹ | [B] / mol L⁻¹ | Initial rate / mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
1 | 0.10 | 0.10 | \(2.0\times10^{-3}\)
2 | 0.20 | 0.10 | \(8.0\times10^{-3}\)
3 | 0.20 | 0.20 | \(1.6\times10^{-2}\)

What are the rate law and the rate constant?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Rate = k[A]²[B]; \(k=2.0\ \mathrm{L^2\,mol^{-2}\,s^{-1}}\).
Concept: The order with respect to each reactant is found by experiment, by changing one concentration at a time. It need not equal the stoichiometric coefficient.
Why: From experiments 1 and 2, [A] doubles at fixed [B] and the rate rises 4 times, so the order in A is 2. From experiments 2 and 3, [B] doubles at fixed [A] and the rate doubles, so the order in B is 1. Then \(k=\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-3}}{(0.10)^2(0.10)}=\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-3}}{1.0\times10^{-3}}=2.0\ \mathrm{L^2\,mol^{-2}\,s^{-1}}\). Check with experiment 3: \(2.0\times(0.20)^2\times0.20=1.6\times10^{-2}\), as measured.
Why not the others: (A) Doubling [A] made the rate four times larger, so the order in A is 2, not 1. (C) It divides the rate by \((0.10)^2\) only and leaves out [B]. (D) It takes the orders from the coefficients in the equation; the data give order 2 in A and 1 in B.
Key point: Orders come from the data, not from the balanced equation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Zero-order kinetics: rate constant and dependence of half-life on initial concentration
questions.question: A reaction is zero order in A. The concentration of A falls from 0.80 mol L⁻¹ to 0.50 mol L⁻¹ in 20 min. What is the rate constant, and what would the half-life be if the initial concentration were 1.60 mol L⁻¹?
options: A) \(0.015\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}\); 26.7 min, the same as for 0.80 mol L⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(0.015\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}\); 53.3 min.
Concept: For a zero-order reaction, \([A]=[A]_0-kt\) and \(t_{1/2}=\dfrac{[A]_0}{2k}\). The half-life is proportional to the initial concentration.
Given: \([A]_0=0.80\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}},\ [A]=0.50\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}},\ t=20\ \mathrm{min};\ \text{new}\ [A]_0=1.60\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(k=\dfrac{[A]_0-[A]}{t};\ t_{1/2}=\dfrac{[A]_0}{2k}\)
Step 1: \(k=\dfrac{0.80-0.50}{20}=0.015\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}\).
Step 2: \(t_{1/2}=\dfrac{1.60}{2\times0.015}=53.3\ \mathrm{min}\).
Why: Doubling the initial concentration doubles the zero-order half-life, from 26.7 min (for 0.80 mol L⁻¹) to 53.3 min.
Why not the others: (A) A constant half-life is the mark of a first-order reaction. (B) It uses 0.50/20 (the concentration left, not the amount used up) for k. (D) It halves the half-life instead of doubling it; for zero order \(t_{1/2}\propto[A]_0\).
Key point: Zero order: \(t_{1/2}=[A]_0/2k\), so it grows with \([A]_0\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Unusually high second ionisation enthalpies of Cr and Cu in the 3d series
questions.question: Among the 3d elements, chromium and copper have unusually high second ionisation enthalpies compared with their neighbours. Which statement gives the correct reason and a linked consequence?
options: A) \(\ce{Cr+}\) is \(3d^5\) and \(\ce{Cu+}\) is \(3d^{10}\); removing a second electron breaks a stable half-filled or filled subshell, so these elements have high second ionisation enthalpies
B) Cr and Cu have the largest atomic radii in the series, so their second electron is held most strongly
C) Cr and Cu have \(4s^2\) configurations, so the second electron comes from a filled 4s orbital
D) Cr and Cu have the lowest nuclear charges in the series, so their ions are very stable
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\ce{Cr+}\) is \(3d^5\) and \(\ce{Cu+}\) is \(3d^{10}\); removing a second electron breaks a stable half-filled or filled subshell, so these elements have high second ionisation enthalpies.
Concept: Cr is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^54s^1\) and Cu is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^1\). The first electron is removed from 4s, leaving \(\ce{Cr+}\) (\(3d^5\)) and \(\ce{Cu+}\) (\(3d^{10}\)). Half-filled and filled subshells have extra stability because of exchange energy.
Why: The second electron must come out of a stable \(3d^5\) or \(3d^{10}\) subshell, so it needs much more energy than for the neighbouring elements, whose second electron comes from 4s.
Why not the others: (B) Atomic radii change only slightly across the 3d series, and a larger radius would lower, not raise, the ionisation enthalpy. (C) Cr and Cu are exceptions with a \(4s^1\) configuration, not \(4s^2\). (D) The nuclear charge rises steadily across the series; Cr and Cu do not have the lowest values.
Key point: Exchange-energy stability of \(d^5\) and \(d^{10}\) raises the second ionisation enthalpy of Cr and Cu.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Colour and spin-only magnetic moment from the d-electron count
questions.question: Which ion is coloured in aqueous solution and has a spin-only magnetic moment of about 3.87 BM?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\ce{Cr^3+}\).
Concept: Spin-only magnetic moment \(\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons. Transition metal ions are coloured when they have partly filled d orbitals, which allow d–d transitions; \(d^0\) and \(d^{10}\) ions are colourless.
Why: \(\sqrt{n(n+2)}=3.87\) gives n = 3. \(\ce{Cr^3+}\) is \(3d^3\), with three unpaired electrons, so \(\mu=\sqrt{15}=3.87\) BM. Its d subshell is partly filled, so it is coloured.
Why not the others: (A) \(\ce{Sc^3+}\) is \(3d^0\): no unpaired electrons and no d–d transition, so it is colourless and diamagnetic. (B) \(\ce{Cu+}\) is \(3d^{10}\): colourless and diamagnetic. (C) \(\ce{Mn^2+}\) is \(3d^5\) with five unpaired electrons: \(\mu=\sqrt{35}=5.92\) BM.
Key point: \(\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\); 3.87 BM ↔ 3 unpaired electrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: IUPAC names of coordination compounds: ligand order, -ate ending and oxidation state
questions.question: Which formula is paired with its correct IUPAC name?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\ce{[Pt(NH3)2Cl(NO2)]}\): diamminechloridonitrito-N-platinum(II).
Concept: IUPAC rules: ligands are named in alphabetical order (ignoring prefixes such as di-, penta-); a complex anion takes the ending -ate (iron → ferrate); the oxidation state of the metal is given in Roman numerals; a ligand bound through N in \(\ce{NO2}\) is nitrito-N.
Why: In C, the ligands in alphabetical order are ammine, chlorido, nitrito-N. The charges are \(2(0)+(-1)+(-1)+x=0\), so x = +2. The complex is neutral, so no -ate ending is used. The name is correct.
Why not the others: (A) The complex is an anion, so iron must be named ferrate: potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III). (B) Ammine comes before chlorido in alphabetical order: pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride. (D) CO is neutral, so nickel is in the 0 oxidation state: tetracarbonylnickel(0).
Key point: Alphabetical ligands, -ate for anionic complexes, oxidation state from charge balance.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Hydrate isomerism of CrCl3·6H2O from the mass of AgCl precipitated
questions.question: A solution containing 0.010 mol of the complex \(\ce{CrCl3.6H2O}\) is treated with excess silver nitrate, and 2.87 g of AgCl (molar mass 143.5 g mol⁻¹) is precipitated at once. What is the formula of the complex, and how is it related to \(\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]Cl3}\)?
options: A) \(\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]Cl3}\); it is an ionisation isomer
B) \(\ce{[Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O}\); it is a hydrate isomer
C) \(\ce{[Cr(H2O)4Cl2]Cl.2H2O}\); it is a hydrate isomer
D) \(\ce{[Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O}\); it is a linkage isomer
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\ce{[Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O}\); it is a hydrate isomer.
Concept: Only chloride ions outside the coordination sphere are precipitated at once by silver nitrate. Hydrate (solvate) isomers differ in whether water is a ligand or is outside the coordination sphere as water of crystallisation.
Given: \(n(\text{complex})=0.010\ \mathrm{mol};\ m(\ce{AgCl})=2.87\ \mathrm g;\ M(\ce{AgCl})=143.5\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: ionisable \(\ce{Cl-}\) per formula unit \(=\dfrac{n(\ce{AgCl})}{n(\text{complex})}\)
Step 1: \(n(\ce{AgCl})=\dfrac{2.87}{143.5}=0.020\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 2: Ionisable chloride per complex = 0.020/0.010 = 2, so one Cl is a ligand: \(\ce{[Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O}\).
Why: The complex keeps six ligands around chromium: five water molecules and one chloride. One water molecule is outside the sphere. Since it differs from \(\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]Cl3}\) only in whether a water or a chloride is the ligand, the two are hydrate isomers.
Why not the others: (A) \(\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]Cl3}\) would give 3 mol AgCl per mol, i.e. 4.31 g. (C) This complex has only one ionisable chloride and would give 1.435 g of AgCl. (D) Linkage isomers differ in the donor atom of an ambidentate ligand (such as \(\ce{NO2-}\)); neither water nor chloride is ambidentate.
Key point: Moles of AgCl precipitated at once = chloride ions outside the coordination sphere.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the slope of a line from the area it encloses with a parabola
questions.question: For \(k>0\), the region bounded by the parabola \(y=x^2\) and the line \(y=kx\) has area 36 square units. What is k?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(6\).
Given: \(y=x^2,\quad y=kx,\quad k>0,\quad\text{area}=36\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{area}=\displaystyle\int_a^b(\text{upper}-\text{lower})\,dx\)
Step 1: \(x^2=kx\Rightarrow x=0\ \text{or}\ x=k;\ \text{on}\ (0,k):\ kx\ge x^2\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\int_0^k(kx-x^2)\,dx=\frac{k^3}{2}-\frac{k^3}{3}=\frac{k^3}{6}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{k^3}{6}=36\Rightarrow k^3=216\Rightarrow k=6\)
Worked derivation: \[\left[\frac{kx^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^k=\frac{k^3}{6}=36\Rightarrow k=\sqrt[3]{216}=6\]
Check: \[k=6:\ \int_0^6(6x-x^2)\,dx=108-72=36\]
Why: \(\text{the region lies between the two intersection points}\ x=0\ \text{and}\ x=k\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{k^3}{3}=36\ \text{uses only the area under the parabola}\); (B) \(\dfrac{k^3}{2}=36\ \text{uses only the area under the line}\); (C) \(k^2=216\ \text{takes a square root instead of a cube root}\).
Key point: \(\text{area between}\ y=x^2\ \text{and}\ y=kx\ \text{is}\ \dfrac{k^3}{6}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Separable differential equation with an initial condition
questions.question: The solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2xy^2\) with \(y(0)=1\) is defined near \(x=0\). What is \(y\left(\tfrac12\right)\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac43\).
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2xy^2,\quad y(0)=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{separate:}\ \dfrac{dy}{y^2}=2x\,dx,\ \text{then integrate both sides}\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\int y^{-2}\,dy=\int2x\,dx\Rightarrow-\frac1y=x^2+C\)
Step 2: \(y(0)=1\Rightarrow-1=C\)
Step 3: \(-\dfrac1y=x^2-1\Rightarrow y=\dfrac1{1-x^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[y\left(\tfrac12\right)=\frac1{1-\tfrac14}=\frac43\]
Check: \[y=\frac1{1-x^2}\Rightarrow y'=\frac{2x}{(1-x^2)^2}=2x\,y^2\ \checkmark,\quad y(0)=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the equation is separable because the right side is a product of a function of}\ x\ \text{and a function of}\ y\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1-x^2\ \text{is}\ \tfrac1y,\ \text{not}\ y\); (C) \(\text{sign error:}\ \tfrac1y=1+x^2\); (D) \(e^{x^2}\ \text{solves}\ y'=2xy,\ \text{not}\ y'=2xy^2\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dy}{y^2}=-\frac1y\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting subsets of one set that are not subsets of another
questions.question: Let \(A=\{x\in\mathbb Z:\ |x-1|\le2\}\) and \(B=\{x\in\mathbb Z:\ x^2<5\}\). How many subsets of A are not subsets of B?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 16.
Given: \(A=\{x\in\mathbb Z:|x-1|\le2\},\quad B=\{x\in\mathbb Z:x^2<5\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(S\subseteq A\ \text{and}\ S\subseteq B\iff S\subseteq A\cap B;\quad|P(X)|=2^{|X|}\)
Step 1: \(|x-1|\le2\iff-1\le x\le3\Rightarrow A=\{-1,0,1,2,3\}\)
Step 2: \(x^2<5\iff-2\le x\le2\ (x\in\mathbb Z)\Rightarrow B=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\)
Step 3: \(A\cap B=\{-1,0,1,2\},\ |A\cap B|=4\)
Worked derivation: \[|P(A)|-|P(A\cap B)|=2^5-2^4=32-16=16\]
Check: \[\text{a subset of}\ A\ \text{is outside}\ P(B)\iff\text{it contains}\ 3:\ 2^4=16\ \text{such subsets}\]
Why: \(3\ \text{is the only element of}\ A\ \text{not in}\ B\)
Why not the others: (A) \(|A|=|B|\ \text{does not make}\ A=B\); (B) \(32-1\ \text{removes only}\ \varnothing\); (D) \(32-8\ \text{miscounts}\ |A\cap B|\ \text{as}\ 3\).
Key point: \(\#\{S\subseteq A:\ S\not\subseteq B\}=2^{|A|}-2^{|A\cap B|}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Intersections of the graph of |x| with a shifted greatest integer function
questions.question: How many solutions does the equation \(|x|=[x]+\tfrac12\) have in the interval \([-3,3]\)? Here \([x]\) is the greatest integer not exceeding x.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3.
Given: \(|x|=[x]+\tfrac12,\quad x\in[-3,3]\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{on}\ [n,n+1),\ [x]=n;\ \text{solve the equation on each such interval}\)
Step 1: \(x\ge0,\ x\in[n,n+1):\ x=n+\tfrac12\in[n,n+1)\ \text{for every}\ n\ge0\)
Step 2: \(x\in[0,3]:\ n=0,1,2\Rightarrow x=\tfrac12,\ \tfrac32,\ \tfrac52\)
Step 3: \(x<0,\ x\in[n,n+1),\ n\le-1:\ -x=n+\tfrac12\Rightarrow x=-n-\tfrac12\ge\tfrac12>0,\ \text{contradiction}\)
Worked derivation: \[\{x\in[-3,3]:\ |x|=[x]+\tfrac12\}=\left\{\tfrac12,\ \tfrac32,\ \tfrac52\right\}\]
Check: \[x=\tfrac32:\ |x|=1.5,\ [x]+\tfrac12=1+0.5=1.5;\quad x=-\tfrac12:\ 0.5\ne-1+0.5\]
Why: \(\text{for}\ x<0,\ |x|>0\ \text{but}\ [x]+\tfrac12\le-\tfrac12<0\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{the step graph is not symmetric about the}\ y\text{-axis}\); (C) \(x=3:\ |3|=3\ne3.5\); (D) \(\text{infinitely many only on}\ [0,\infty);\ \text{in}\ [-3,3]\ \text{there are 3}\).
Key point: \(\text{the line}\ y=x\ \text{meets each step}\ y=n+\tfrac12\ \text{at its midpoint}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Angle between two position vectors using the tangent of a difference
questions.question: Let O be the origin, \(A=(2,1)\) and \(B=(1,3)\). What is the angle AOB?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac\pi4\).
Given: \(O=(0,0),\ A=(2,1),\ B=(1,3)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tan(\beta-\alpha)=\dfrac{\tan\beta-\tan\alpha}{1+\tan\beta\tan\alpha}\)
Step 1: \(\tan\alpha=\dfrac12\ (\text{line}\ OA),\quad\tan\beta=3\ (\text{line}\ OB)\)
Step 2: \(\tan(\beta-\alpha)=\dfrac{3-\tfrac12}{1+\tfrac32}=\dfrac{5/2}{5/2}=1\)
Worked derivation: \[\angle AOB=\beta-\alpha=\tan^{-1}1=\frac\pi4\quad(0<\beta-\alpha<\tfrac\pi2)\]
Check: \[\cos\angle AOB=\frac{(2,1)\cdot(1,3)}{\sqrt5\,\sqrt{10}}=\frac5{5\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\Rightarrow\frac\pi4\]
Why: \(\text{the angle between the lines is the difference of their inclinations}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tan\tfrac\pi6=\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\ne1\); (B) \(\tan\tfrac\pi3=\sqrt3\ne1\); (D) \(\text{uses}\ \tan(\alpha+\beta)=\dfrac{3+\frac12}{1-\frac32}=-7\).
Key point: \(\tan(\beta-\alpha)\ \text{gives the angle between two lines through the origin}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding a complex number from its modulus and principal argument
questions.question: A complex number \(z=a+ib\) has \(|z|=2\) and principal argument \(\dfrac{2\pi}3\). What are a and b?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(a=-1,\ b=\sqrt3\).
Given: \(r=2,\quad\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}3\)
Formula/Principle: \(z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\)
Step 1: \(a=2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}3=2\left(-\tfrac12\right)=-1\)
Step 2: \(b=2\sin\dfrac{2\pi}3=2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}2=\sqrt3\)
Worked derivation: \[z=2\left(\cos\tfrac{2\pi}3+i\sin\tfrac{2\pi}3\right)=-1+i\sqrt3\]
Check: \[|z|=\sqrt{1+3}=2,\quad z\ \text{in quadrant II},\ \tan^{-1}\tfrac{\sqrt3}{1}=\tfrac\pi3\Rightarrow\arg z=\pi-\tfrac\pi3=\tfrac{2\pi}3\]
Why: \(\tfrac{2\pi}3\ \text{lies in the second quadrant:}\ a<0,\ b>0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\arg=\tfrac\pi3\); (B) \(\arg=\tfrac{5\pi}6\); (C) \(\arg=-\tfrac{2\pi}3\).
Key point: \(a=r\cos\theta,\ b=r\sin\theta\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Locus |z − 1| = k|z + 1| and its special case k = 1
questions.question: For a real number \(k>0\), consider the locus of z satisfying \(|z-1|=k\,|z+1|\). For which value of k is the locus a straight line, and which line is it?
options: D) No value of k; the locus is always a circle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(k=1\); the imaginary axis.
Given: \(|z-1|=k|z+1|,\quad k>0,\quad z=x+iy\)
Formula/Principle: \(|z-a|^2=(x-\operatorname{Re}a)^2+(y-\operatorname{Im}a)^2\)
Step 1: \((x-1)^2+y^2=k^2\left[(x+1)^2+y^2\right]\)
Step 2: \((1-k^2)(x^2+y^2)-2(1+k^2)x+(1-k^2)=0\)
Step 3: \(k\ne1:\ \text{circle};\quad k=1:\ -4x=0\Rightarrow x=0\)
Worked derivation: \[k=1:\ (x-1)^2+y^2=(x+1)^2+y^2\iff-2x=2x\iff x=0\]
Check: \[z=3i:\ |3i-1|=\sqrt{10}=|3i+1|\ \checkmark;\quad z=1:\ 0\ne2\]
Why: \(k=1\ \text{means equal distance from}\ 1\ \text{and}\ -1:\ \text{the perpendicular bisector}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{points on the real axis other than}\ 0\ \text{are not equidistant from}\ \pm1\); (C) \(k=2:\ 3(x^2+y^2)+10x+3=0\ \text{is a circle}\); (D) \(k=1\ \text{gives a line}\).
Key point: \(|z-a|=|z-b|\ \text{is the perpendicular bisector of}\ ab\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Arrangements of a word with repeated letters when the vowels are not all together
questions.question: In how many arrangements of all the letters of the word SCIENCE do the three vowels not all come together?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1080.
Given: \(\text{SCIENCE: 7 letters};\ C\times2,\ E\times2;\ \text{vowels}\ I,E,E\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{n!}{p!\,q!}\ \text{for repeated letters};\ \text{wanted}=\text{total}-\text{vowels together}\)
Step 1: \(\text{total}=\dfrac{7!}{2!\,2!}=\dfrac{5040}4=1260\)
Step 2: \(\text{block}\ [IEE]+S,C,N,C:\ \dfrac{5!}{2!}=60;\ \text{inside block:}\ \dfrac{3!}{2!}=3\Rightarrow180\)
Worked derivation: \[1260-60\times3=1260-180=1080\]
Check: \[\text{fraction together}=\frac{180}{1260}=\frac17;\ \text{as a check,}\ \frac{5!\,3!}{7!}=\frac{720}{5040}=\frac17\]
Why: \(\text{count the complement, then subtract}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1260\ \text{is the total with no restriction}\); (C) \(7!-5!\,3!\ \text{ignores the repeated letters}\); (D) \(1260-60\ \text{forgets the 3 orders inside the block}\).
Key point: \(\text{not all together}=\text{total}-\text{together}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Term independent of x in a binomial expansion
questions.question: What is the term independent of x in the expansion of \(\left(x^2-\dfrac2x\right)^9\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(5376\).
Given: \(\left(x^2-\dfrac2x\right)^9\)
Formula/Principle: \(T_{r+1}=\binom9r(x^2)^{9-r}\left(-\dfrac2x\right)^r\)
Step 1: \(T_{r+1}=\binom9r(-2)^rx^{18-3r}\)
Step 2: \(18-3r=0\Rightarrow r=6\)
Step 3: \(\dbinom96=84,\quad(-2)^6=64\)
Worked derivation: \[T_7=\binom96(-2)^6=84\times64=5376\]
Check: \[r=6\ \text{is even, so the sign is}\ +;\ \text{power of}\ x:\ 2(3)-6=0\]
Why: \(\text{only}\ r=6\ \text{gives}\ x^0\)
Why not the others: (A) \((-2)^6>0\); (B) \(\binom93\,2^3=672\ \text{uses}\ r=3\); (C) \(\text{leaves out}\ (-2)^6\).
Key point: \(\text{set the power of}\ x\ \text{in}\ T_{r+1}\ \text{to zero}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Eccentricity and latus rectum of an ellipse from its foci and a point on it
questions.question: An ellipse has its centre at the origin and its axes along the coordinate axes. Its foci are \((\pm3,0)\) and it passes through \(\left(4,\tfrac{12}5\right)\). What are its eccentricity and the length of its latus rectum?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac35\) and \(\dfrac{32}5\).
Given: \(c=3,\quad P=\left(4,\tfrac{12}5\right)\)
Formula/Principle: \(PF_1+PF_2=2a;\quad b^2=a^2-c^2;\quad e=\dfrac ca;\quad\text{LR}=\dfrac{2b^2}a\)
Step 1: \(PF_1=\sqrt{(4-3)^2+\left(\tfrac{12}5\right)^2}=\sqrt{\tfrac{169}{25}}=\tfrac{13}5\)
Step 2: \(PF_2=\sqrt{(4+3)^2+\left(\tfrac{12}5\right)^2}=\sqrt{\tfrac{1369}{25}}=\tfrac{37}5\)
Step 3: \(2a=\tfrac{50}5=10\Rightarrow a=5,\quad b^2=25-9=16\)
Worked derivation: \[e=\frac35,\qquad\text{LR}=\frac{2\times16}{5}=\frac{32}5\]
Check: \[\frac{16}{25}+\frac{144/25}{16}=\frac{16}{25}+\frac9{25}=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the sum of focal distances fixes}\ a\ \text{directly}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\dfrac{2a^2}b=\dfrac{50}4\ \text{swaps}\ a\ \text{and}\ b\); (C) \(\dfrac cb=\dfrac34\ \text{divides by}\ b\); (D) \(\dfrac ba=\dfrac45\ \text{is not}\ e\).
Key point: \(PF_1+PF_2=2a,\ e=\dfrac ca\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding a parameter from a trigonometric limit
questions.question: For a positive constant a, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos ax}{x\sin x}=8\). What is a?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4.
Given: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos ax}{x\sin x}=8,\quad a>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(1-\cos ax=2\sin^2\dfrac{ax}2;\quad\displaystyle\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\sin t}t=1\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1-\cos ax}{x\sin x}=\dfrac{2\sin^2(ax/2)}{x^2}\cdot\dfrac{x}{\sin x}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{2\sin^2(ax/2)}{x^2}=2\cdot\dfrac{a^2}4\left(\dfrac{\sin(ax/2)}{ax/2}\right)^2\to\dfrac{a^2}2\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{a^2}2\times1=8\Rightarrow a^2=16\Rightarrow a=4\]
Check: \[a=4:\ \lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos4x}{x\sin x}=\frac{16}2=8\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(1-\cos ax\approx\dfrac{a^2x^2}2\ \text{and}\ x\sin x\approx x^2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the limit is}\ \tfrac{a^2}2,\ \text{not}\ a\); (B) \(\text{uses}\ \tfrac a2=8\); (D) \(\text{uses}\ a^2=8,\ \text{forgetting the factor}\ \tfrac12\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos ax}{x^2}=\frac{a^2}2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding an unknown observation from the range, then the mean deviation about the median
questions.question: The observations 2, 4, 6, 8 and x, where \(x>8\), have range 12. What are x and the mean deviation about the median?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 14 and 3.2.
Given: \(2,4,6,8,x;\quad x>8;\quad\text{range}=12\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{range}=\max-\min;\quad\text{M.D.}(M)=\dfrac1n\sum|x_i-M|\)
Step 1: \(x-2=12\Rightarrow x=14\)
Step 2: \(\text{ordered: }2,4,6,8,14\Rightarrow M=6\)
Step 3: \(|x_i-6|:\ 4,2,0,2,8;\ \text{sum}=16\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{M.D.}(M)=\frac{16}5=3.2\]
Check: \[\bar x=\frac{34}5=6.8;\ \sum|x_i-6.8|=16.8>16\ \text{(the median minimises the sum)}\]
Why: \(\text{the median is the middle value of the ordered data}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3.36\ \text{is about the mean}\ 6.8\); (C) \(\text{takes the largest value as}\ 12\); (D) \(16\ \text{is the sum, not divided by}\ 5\).
Key point: \(\text{M.D. about the median}=\dfrac{\sum|x_i-M|}n\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Addition rule: probability of exactly one event and test of mutual exclusivity
questions.question: For events A and B, \(P(A)=0.4\), \(P(B)=0.5\) and \(P(A\cup B)=0.7\). What is the probability that exactly one of A and B occurs, and are A and B mutually exclusive?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.5; not mutually exclusive.
Given: \(P(A)=0.4,\ P(B)=0.5,\ P(A\cup B)=0.7\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B);\quad P(\text{exactly one})=P(A\cup B)-P(A\cap B)\)
Step 1: \(P(A\cap B)=0.4+0.5-0.7=0.2\)
Step 2: \(P(A\cap B)\ne0\Rightarrow\text{not mutually exclusive}\)
Worked derivation: \[P(\text{exactly one})=0.7-0.2=0.5\]
Check: \[P(A)-P(A\cap B)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)=0.2+0.3=0.5\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{mutually exclusive}\iff P(A\cap B)=0\)
Why not the others: (B) \(0.7\ \text{is}\ P(\text{at least one})\); (C) \(0.3\ \text{is}\ P(\text{neither})\); (D) \(0.4+0.5\ \text{ignores the overlap}\).
Key point: \(P(\text{exactly one})=P(A)+P(B)-2P(A\cap B)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Probability that two balls drawn have the same colour: solving for the number of balls
questions.question: A bag has n red balls and 3 blue balls, where \(n\ge1\). Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. The probability that both are of the same colour is \(\tfrac12\). What are the possible values of n?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1 and 6.
Given: \(n\ \text{red},\ 3\ \text{blue};\ P(\text{same colour})=\tfrac12\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=\dfrac{\binom n2+\binom32}{\binom{n+3}2}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{\tfrac{n(n-1)}2+3}{\tfrac{(n+3)(n+2)}2}=\dfrac12\Rightarrow2\left[n(n-1)+6\right]=(n+3)(n+2)\)
Step 2: \(2n^2-2n+12=n^2+5n+6\Rightarrow n^2-7n+6=0\)
Worked derivation: \[(n-1)(n-6)=0\Rightarrow n=1\ \text{or}\ n=6\]
Check: \[n=1:\ \frac{0+3}{6}=\frac12;\qquad n=6:\ \frac{15+3}{36}=\frac12\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{both roots are positive integers, so both are allowed}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(n=1\ \text{also works}\); (B) \(n=6\ \text{also works}\); (C) \(n=2:\ \tfrac{1+3}{10}=\tfrac25;\ n=3:\ \tfrac{3+3}{15}=\tfrac25\).
Key point: \(\text{count both same-colour cases, then solve the quadratic and test each root}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting 3 × 3 matrices with entries from {−1, 0, 1} that are symmetric or skew-symmetric
questions.question: How many \(3\times3\) matrices with every entry in \(\{-1,0,1\}\) are symmetric or skew-symmetric?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 755.
Given: \(3\times3,\ a_{ij}\in\{-1,0,1\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(|S\cup K|=|S|+|K|-|S\cap K|\)
Step 1: \(\text{symmetric: diagonal (3) and upper triangle (3) are free}\Rightarrow|S|=3^6=729\)
Step 2: \(\text{skew-symmetric: diagonal}=0,\ \text{upper triangle (3) free}\Rightarrow|K|=3^3=27\)
Step 3: \(A=A^T=-A^T\Rightarrow A=O\Rightarrow|S\cap K|=1\)
Worked derivation: \[|S\cup K|=729+27-1=755\]
Check: \[\text{the zero matrix is the only one counted twice}\]
Why: \(\text{entries below the diagonal are fixed by those above it}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{counts the zero matrix twice}\); (C) \(\text{counts only the symmetric ones}\); (D) \(729-1\ \text{counts symmetric but not skew-symmetric}\).
Key point: \(\text{symmetric and skew-symmetric}\iff\text{zero matrix}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Product of two non-zero matrices that is the zero matrix: projections onto the axes
questions.question: The matrix A maps every point \((x,y)\) of the plane to its projection \((x,0)\) on the x-axis, and the matrix B maps \((x,y)\) to its projection \((0,y)\) on the y-axis. What is the product AB?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The zero matrix.
Given: \(A\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}x\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad B\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\y\end{pmatrix}\)
Formula/Principle: \((AB)v=A(Bv)\)
Step 1: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(A(Bv)=A\begin{pmatrix}0\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}\ \text{for every}\ v\)
Worked derivation: \[AB=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\]
Check: \[(AB)\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}=A\begin{pmatrix}0\\5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
Why: \(\text{a point already on the}\ y\text{-axis projects to the origin on the}\ x\text{-axis}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(AB\ \text{sends}\ (1,0)\ \text{to}\ (0,0),\ \text{not}\ (1,0)\); (B) \(A\ne O\); (D) \(B\ne O\).
Key point: \(AB=O\ \text{does not imply}\ A=O\ \text{or}\ B=O\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Points of non-differentiability of a product containing an absolute value
questions.question: Let \(f(x)=(x-1)\,|x^2-3x+2|\) for all real x. Where is f not differentiable?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Only at \(x=2\).
Given: \(f(x)=(x-1)|x^2-3x+2|=(x-1)|x-1|\,|x-2|\)
Formula/Principle: \(g(x)=(x-a)|x-a|\ \text{is differentiable at}\ a;\ |x-b|\ \text{has a corner at}\ b\)
Step 1: \(\text{near}\ x=1:\ f=(x-1)|x-1|\cdot|x-2|,\ \text{product of differentiable functions}\)
Step 2: \(\text{near}\ x=2:\ f(x)=h(x)|x-2|,\ h(x)=(x-1)|x-1|,\ h(2)=1\ne0\)
Step 3: \(f'(2^+)=h(2)=1,\quad f'(2^-)=-h(2)=-1\)
Worked derivation: \[f'(1)=\lim_{x\to1}\frac{(x-1)|x-1||x-2|}{x-1}=\lim_{x\to1}|x-1||x-2|=0;\qquad f'(2^\pm)=\pm1\]
Check: \[f\ \text{is continuous everywhere, so a corner, not a jump, occurs at}\ x=2\]
Why: \(\text{a factor that vanishes at the corner smooths it; a non-zero factor keeps it}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(f'(2^+)\ne f'(2^-)\); (C) \(f'(1)=0\ \text{exists}\); (D) \(x=1\ \text{is smooth and}\ x=2\ \text{is the corner}\).
Key point: \((x-a)|x-a|\ \text{is differentiable;}\ c\,|x-a|\ (c\ne0)\ \text{is not}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Derivative of an inverse trigonometric function by substitution
questions.question: For \(|x|<1\), let \(y=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)\). What is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac2{1+x^2}\).
Given: \(y=\sin^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2},\quad|x|<1\)
Formula/Principle: \(x=\tan\theta\Rightarrow\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}=\sin2\theta\)
Step 1: \(|x|<1\Rightarrow\theta\in\left(-\tfrac\pi4,\tfrac\pi4\right)\Rightarrow2\theta\in\left(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2\right)\)
Step 2: \(y=\sin^{-1}(\sin2\theta)=2\theta=2\tan^{-1}x\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{d}{dx}\left(2\tan^{-1}x\right)=\frac2{1+x^2}\]
Check: \[x=0:\ y\approx\sin^{-1}(2x)\approx2x\Rightarrow y'(0)=2=\frac2{1+0}\]
Why: \(2\theta\ \text{lies in the principal range of}\ \sin^{-1}\ \text{only when}\ |x|<1\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{drops the factor 2 from}\ 2\tan^{-1}x\); (C) \(\text{that is the derivative for}\ |x|>1\); (D) \(\text{differentiates as if}\ y=2\sin^{-1}x\).
Key point: \(\sin^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}=2\tan^{-1}x\ \text{for}\ |x|\le1\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Intervals of increase and decrease of x² e^(−x)
questions.question: On which intervals is \(f(x)=x^2e^{-x}\) increasing, and on which is it decreasing?
options: D) Increasing on \([0,2]\); decreasing on \((-\infty,0]\) and on \([2,\infty)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Increasing on \([0,2]\); decreasing on \((-\infty,0]\) and on \([2,\infty)\).
Given: \(f(x)=x^2e^{-x}\)
Formula/Principle: \(f'>0\Rightarrow\text{increasing};\ f'<0\Rightarrow\text{decreasing}\)
Step 1: \(f'(x)=2xe^{-x}-x^2e^{-x}=x(2-x)e^{-x}\)
Step 2: \(e^{-x}>0;\ \text{sign of}\ f'=\text{sign of}\ x(2-x)\)
Step 3: \(x<0:\ f'<0;\quad0<x<2:\ f'>0;\quad x>2:\ f'<0\)
Worked derivation: \[f'(x)=x(2-x)e^{-x}\ \Rightarrow\ \uparrow\ \text{on}\ [0,2],\ \downarrow\ \text{on}\ (-\infty,0]\cup[2,\infty)\]
Check: \[f(0)=0,\ f(2)=4e^{-2}\approx0.54,\ f(4)=16e^{-4}\approx0.29:\ \text{rises then falls}\]
Why: \(\text{the factor}\ e^{-x}\ \text{eventually beats}\ x^2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(f'(-1)=-3e<0\ \text{on}\ (-\infty,0)\); (B) \(f'(3)=-3e^{-3}<0\); (C) \(\text{reverses the signs of}\ f'\).
Key point: \(\text{factor}\ f'\ \text{fully and read its sign on each interval}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Reduction formula by integration by parts for the integral of x^n e^x from 0 to 1
questions.question: Let \(I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1x^ne^x\,dx\) for \(n\ge0\). Integration by parts gives \(I_n=e-nI_{n-1}\) for \(n\ge1\). What is \(I_3\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(6-2e\).
Given: \(I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1x^ne^x\,dx,\quad I_n=e-nI_{n-1}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du\ \text{with}\ u=x^n,\ dv=e^xdx\)
Step 1: \(I_0=\displaystyle\int_0^1e^x\,dx=e-1\)
Step 2: \(I_1=e-1\cdot I_0=e-(e-1)=1\)
Step 3: \(I_2=e-2I_1=e-2\)
Worked derivation: \[I_3=e-3I_2=e-3(e-2)=6-2e\]
Check: \[6-2e\approx0.563;\ \ 0<x^3e^x<e\ \text{on}\ (0,1)\ \text{and}\ \int_0^1x^3e\,dx=\tfrac e4\approx0.68>0.563>0\]
Why: \(\left[x^ne^x\right]_0^1=e\ \text{for}\ n\ge1\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{sign error:}\ 2e-6<0,\ \text{but}\ I_3>0\); (B) \(e-2=I_2\); (D) \(\text{uses}\ I_2=1\ \text{in place of}\ e-2\).
Key point: \(I_n=e-nI_{n-1},\ I_0=e-1\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Huygens construction for refraction: graph of sin r against sin i
questions.question: A plane wavefront travels from air, where its speed is c, into glass, where its speed is \(\tfrac23c\). Using Huygens' construction, sin r is plotted against sin i, where i is the angle of incidence and r the angle of refraction. What does the graph look like?
options: A) A straight line through the origin with slope \(\tfrac23\)
B) A straight line through the origin with slope \(\tfrac32\)
C) A straight line through the origin with slope 1, because the frequency does not change
D) A curve that becomes vertical at \(\sin i\approx0.67\), where total internal reflection begins
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A straight line through the origin with slope \(\tfrac23\).
Given: \(v_1=c,\quad v_2=\tfrac23c\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Huygens:}\ \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\)
Step 1: \(\text{in the time}\ \tau\ \text{the wavelet in air covers}\ BC=v_1\tau,\ \text{the wavelet in glass covers}\ AE=v_2\tau\)
Step 2: \(\sin i=\dfrac{BC}{AC},\quad\sin r=\dfrac{AE}{AC}\Rightarrow\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\)
Worked derivation: \[\sin r=\frac{v_2}{v_1}\sin i=\frac23\sin i\]
Check: \[\sin i=0.9\Rightarrow\sin r=0.6\le1;\ \text{a refracted ray exists for every}\ i\ \text{(rarer to denser)}\]
Why: \(\text{the wave slows down in glass, so it bends towards the normal}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses}\ \tfrac{v_1}{v_2};\ \text{that is the slope of}\ \sin i\ \text{against}\ \sin r\); (C) \(\text{frequency is unchanged, but speed and wavelength change}\); (D) \(\text{total internal reflection needs travel from the denser to the rarer medium}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}=\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Carrier concentrations in an n-type semiconductor from the law of mass action
questions.question: Pure silicon at 300 K has an intrinsic carrier concentration \(n_i=1.5\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\). It is doped with arsenic at \(5.0\times10^{22}\) atoms per cubic metre, and every arsenic atom is ionised. What are the electron and hole concentrations?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(n_e=5.0\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}},\ n_h=4.5\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\).
Given: \(n_i=1.5\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}},\quad N_D=5.0\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\ \text{(pentavalent As, donor)}\)
Formula/Principle: \(n_en_h=n_i^2;\quad n_e\approx N_D\ \text{when}\ N_D\gg n_i\)
Step 1: \(n_e\approx5.0\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\)
Step 2: \(n_i^2=(1.5\times10^{16})^2=2.25\times10^{32}\ \mathrm{m^{-6}}\)
Worked derivation: \[n_h=\frac{n_i^2}{n_e}=\frac{2.25\times10^{32}}{5.0\times10^{22}}=4.5\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\]
Check: \[n_en_h=5.0\times10^{22}\times4.5\times10^{9}=2.25\times10^{32}=n_i^2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{extra electrons recombine with holes, so the hole density falls below}\ n_i\)
Why not the others: (A) \(n_h=n_i\ \text{only in a pure crystal}\); (C) \(\text{arsenic is a donor, so electrons are the majority}\); (D) \(\dfrac{n_i}{n_e}\ \text{is not}\ \dfrac{n_i^2}{n_e}\).
Key point: \(n_en_h=n_i^2\ \text{in thermal equilibrium}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Significant figures when a measurement is divided by an exact count
questions.question: A stack of exactly 250 identical sheets of paper is measured with a vernier calliper to be 2.54 cm thick. How should the thickness of one sheet be reported?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.0102 cm.
Given: \(T=2.54\ \mathrm{cm}\ (3\ \text{s.f.}),\quad N=250\ (\text{exact count})\)
Formula/Principle: \(t=\dfrac TN;\ \text{an exact count has unlimited significant figures; keep the s.f. of the measurement}\)
Step 1: \(t=\dfrac{2.54}{250}=0.01016\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 2: \(\text{3 s.f. (from 2.54)}\Rightarrow t=0.0102\ \mathrm{cm}=1.02\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Worked derivation: \[t=\frac{2.54\ \mathrm{cm}}{250}=1.016\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{cm}\ \to\ 1.02\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{cm}\]
Check: \[\text{leading zeros are not significant: in 0.0102 the figures 1, 0, 2 are significant (3)}\]
Why: \(\text{counting gives an exact number, so it does not limit the precision}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{keeps 4 s.f. from a 3 s.f. measurement}\); (B) \(\text{treats 250 as 2 s.f.}\); (C) \(\text{1 s.f. throws away reliable figures}\).
Key point: \(\text{exact counts do not reduce significant figures}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Average velocity and average speed when the motion reverses
questions.question: A particle moves along the x-axis with \(x(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t\), where x is in metres and t in seconds. What are its average velocity and its average speed over the interval from \(t=0\) to \(t=3\ \mathrm s\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(0\) and \(\tfrac83\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
Given: \(x(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t,\quad0\le t\le3\ \mathrm s\)
Formula/Principle: \(\bar v=\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t};\quad\text{average speed}=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\Delta t};\quad v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}\)
Step 1: \(x(0)=0,\quad x(3)=27-54+27=0\Rightarrow\Delta x=0\)
Step 2: \(v=3t^2-12t+9=3(t-1)(t-3)=0\Rightarrow\text{turns at}\ t=1\ \mathrm s,\ x(1)=4\ \mathrm m\)
Step 3: \(\text{distance}=|4-0|+|0-4|=8\ \mathrm m\)
Worked derivation: \[\bar v=\frac{0}{3}=0,\qquad\text{average speed}=\frac{8}{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\]
Check: \[v(0.5)=3.75>0\ \text{(moving out)},\ v(2)=-3<0\ \text{(moving back)}\]
Why: \(\text{velocity counts displacement; speed counts the whole path}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses distance for velocity}\); (C) \(\text{zero displacement does not mean zero distance}\); (D) \(\text{counts only the outward 4 m}\).
Key point: \(|\bar v|\le\text{average speed};\ \text{equal only without reversal}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Impulse and average force measured for a ball rebounding from a wall
questions.question: In an experiment, a ball of mass 0.15 kg hits a wall at 20 m/s along the normal and rebounds along the same line at 15 m/s. A force sensor on the wall records a contact time of 0.050 s. What are the magnitude of the impulse on the ball and the average force on it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(5.25\ \mathrm{N\,s}\) and \(105\ \mathrm N\).
Given: \(m=0.15\ \mathrm{kg},\ u=+20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\ (\text{towards wall}),\ v=-15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\ \Delta t=0.050\ \mathrm s\)
Formula/Principle: \(J=\Delta p=m(v-u);\quad F_{\text{avg}}=\dfrac{J}{\Delta t}\)
Step 1: \(J=0.15\,(-15-20)=-5.25\ \mathrm{N\,s}\Rightarrow|J|=5.25\ \mathrm{N\,s}\)
Step 2: \(F_{\text{avg}}=\dfrac{5.25}{0.050}=105\ \mathrm N\ \text{(away from the wall)}\)
Worked derivation: \[|J|=m(|u|+|v|)=0.15\times35=5.25\ \mathrm{N\,s},\qquad F=\frac{5.25}{0.050}=105\ \mathrm N\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\frac{\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}}{\mathrm s}=\mathrm N;\ \text{a rebound gives more impulse than stopping (3.0 N s)}\]
Why: \(\text{velocity reverses, so the speeds add}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{subtracts the speeds instead of the velocities}\); (C) \(\text{multiplies by}\ \Delta t\ \text{instead of dividing}\); (D) \(\text{uses only the momentum lost in stopping}\).
Key point: \(\text{rebound:}\ |\Delta p|=m(|u|+|v|)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Elastic potential energy of two springs under the same force and under the same extension
questions.question: Spring 1 has spring constant 200 N/m and spring 2 has 800 N/m. Compare the elastic potential energies stored (a) when both are stretched by the same force, and (b) when both are stretched by the same extension.
options: A) Spring 1 stores more in both cases
B) Spring 2 stores more in both cases
C) They store equal energy in both cases
D) (a) Spring 1 stores 4 times as much; (b) spring 2 stores 4 times as much
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (a) Spring 1 stores 4 times as much; (b) spring 2 stores 4 times as much.
Given: \(k_1=200\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}},\quad k_2=800\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(U=\tfrac12kx^2;\quad F=kx\Rightarrow U=\dfrac{F^2}{2k}\)
Step 1: \(\text{same}\ F:\ \dfrac{U_1}{U_2}=\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}=\dfrac{800}{200}=4\)
Step 2: \(\text{same}\ x:\ \dfrac{U_2}{U_1}=\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}=4\)
Worked derivation: \[F=40\ \mathrm N:\ U_1=\frac{1600}{400}=4\ \mathrm J,\ U_2=\frac{1600}{1600}=1\ \mathrm J;\quad x=0.1\ \mathrm m:\ U_1=1\ \mathrm J,\ U_2=4\ \mathrm J\]
Check: \[\text{same}\ F:\ x_1=0.2\ \mathrm m,\ x_2=0.05\ \mathrm m;\ U=\tfrac12Fx:\ 4\ \mathrm J\ \text{and}\ 1\ \mathrm J\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at the same force the softer spring stretches more}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{fails for same}\ x\); (B) \(\text{fails for same}\ F\); (C) \(U\ \text{depends on}\ k\ \text{in both cases}\).
Key point: \(\text{same}\ F:\ U\propto\tfrac1k;\quad\text{same}\ x:\ U\propto k\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.sub_topic: Support forces on a plank in equilibrium from force and torque balance
questions.question: A uniform plank of length 4.0 m and mass 20 kg rests on two supports at its ends. A person of mass 60 kg stands 1.0 m from the left end. Take \(g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). What are the forces exerted by the left and right supports?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 550 N and 250 N.
Given: \(L=4.0\ \mathrm m,\ W_p=200\ \mathrm N\ \text{at}\ 2.0\ \mathrm m,\ W=600\ \mathrm N\ \text{at}\ 1.0\ \mathrm m\ \text{from left}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sum F_y=0,\quad\sum\tau=0\ \text{about any point}\)
Step 1: \(\text{torques about the left end:}\ R_R(4.0)=200(2.0)+600(1.0)=1000\ \mathrm{N\,m}\)
Step 2: \(R_R=250\ \mathrm N\)
Step 3: \(R_L=800-250=550\ \mathrm N\)
Worked derivation: \[R_R=\frac{400+600}{4.0}=250\ \mathrm N,\qquad R_L=(200+600)-250=550\ \mathrm N\]
Check: \[\text{about the right end:}\ R_L(4.0)=200(2.0)+600(3.0)=2200\Rightarrow R_L=550\ \mathrm N\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the person is nearer the left end, so the left support carries more}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores where the person stands}\); (B) \(\text{leaves out the weight of the plank}\); (D) \(\text{swaps the two supports}\).
Key point: \(\text{take torques about one support to remove its unknown force}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Equal fractional change of g at a small height and at a depth
questions.question: Take the radius of the Earth as 6400 km. By about what percentage does g decrease at a height of 32 km above the surface, and at about what depth below the surface is the decrease the same?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1%; 64 km.
Given: \(R=6400\ \mathrm{km},\quad h=32\ \mathrm{km}\ll R\)
Formula/Principle: \(g_h\approx g\left(1-\dfrac{2h}R\right);\quad g_d=g\left(1-\dfrac dR\right)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{\Delta g}{g}=\dfrac{2h}R=\dfrac{2\times32}{6400}=0.01=1\%\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac dR=\dfrac{2h}R\Rightarrow d=2h\)
Worked derivation: \[d=2\times32=64\ \mathrm{km},\qquad\frac{d}{R}=\frac{64}{6400}=1\%\]
Check: \[\text{exact: }\left(\frac{6400}{6432}\right)^2=0.99007\Rightarrow0.99\%\approx1\%\]
Why: \(g\ \text{falls twice as fast with height as with depth near the surface}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses}\ \tfrac hR\ \text{for height and}\ d=h\); (C) \(d=\tfrac h2\ \text{inverts the factor 2}\); (D) \(\text{uses}\ \tfrac{4h}R\).
Key point: \(\text{same}\ g\ \text{at height}\ h\ \text{and depth}\ d=2h\ (h\ll R)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Draining tank with Torricelli efflux: which graph is a straight line
questions.question: Water drains through a small hole at the bottom of a wide open tank of constant cross-section. The area of the hole is much smaller than that of the tank. Let h be the height of the water above the hole and v the speed of efflux. Which of these graphs is a straight line?
options: D) volume flow rate against h
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) v against time.
Given: \(\text{tank area}\ A,\ \text{hole area}\ a\ll A,\ \text{height}\ h(t)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Torricelli:}\ v=\sqrt{2gh};\quad\text{continuity:}\ -A\dfrac{dh}{dt}=av\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dh}{dt}=-\dfrac aA\sqrt{2gh}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{g}{\sqrt{2gh}}\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac g{v}\left(-\dfrac aA v\right)=-\dfrac{ag}A\)
Worked derivation: \[v(t)=v_0-\frac{ag}{A}t\quad\Rightarrow\quad h(t)=\frac{v(t)^2}{2g}\ \text{(a parabola in}\ t)\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\frac{ag}{A}\ \text{has units of}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}};\ v\ \text{falls at a constant rate}\]
Why: \(\text{the efflux speed falls at a steady rate, like uniform deceleration}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(h\propto(v_0-kt)^2\ \text{is a parabola}\); (C) \(v\propto\sqrt h\ \text{is a curve}\); (D) \(av\propto\sqrt h\ \text{is a curve}\).
Key point: \(v=\sqrt{2gh}\ \text{and}\ A\,dh=-av\,dt\ \Rightarrow\ dv/dt=\text{constant}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Mixing ice and water: whether all the ice melts and the final temperature
questions.question: 200 g of water at 40 °C is in an insulated vessel of negligible heat capacity. In case 1, 50 g of ice at 0 °C is added; in case 2, 150 g of ice at 0 °C is added instead. Take the specific heat of water as 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and the latent heat of fusion of ice as 336 J g⁻¹. What is the final state in each case?
options: A) Case 1: 16 °C; case 2: 0 °C with all the ice melted
D) Case 1: 16 °C; case 2: 0 °C with 50 g of ice left
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Case 1: 16 °C; case 2: 0 °C with 50 g of ice left.
Given: \(m_w=200\ \mathrm g,\ T_w=40\ ^\circ\mathrm C,\ c=4.2\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}K^{-1}},\ L=336\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{heat lost}=\text{heat gained};\ Q=mL\ \text{for melting},\ Q=mc\Delta T\ \text{for warming}\)
Step 1: \(\text{heat available to cool water to}\ 0\ ^\circ\mathrm C:\ 200\times4.2\times40=33600\ \mathrm J\Rightarrow\text{can melt}\ \dfrac{33600}{336}=100\ \mathrm g\)
Step 2: \(\text{case 1: melting 50 g uses}\ 16800\ \mathrm J;\ 250\times4.2\times T=33600-16800\)
Step 3: \(\text{case 2: only 100 g of 150 g melts}\Rightarrow0\ ^\circ\mathrm C,\ 50\ \mathrm g\ \text{left}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{case 1: }200(4.2)(40-T)=50(336)+50(4.2)T\Rightarrow33600-840T=16800+210T\Rightarrow T=16\ ^\circ\mathrm C\]
Check: \[\text{case 1: lost }200(4.2)(24)=20160\ \mathrm J;\ \text{gained }16800+50(4.2)(16)=20160\ \mathrm J\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the mixture stays at}\ 0\ ^\circ\mathrm C\ \text{while ice and water coexist}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{only 100 g can melt in case 2}\); (B) \(\text{ignores latent heat}\); (C) \(\text{in case 1 all 50 g melts with heat to spare}\).
Key point: \(\text{first check how much ice the available heat can melt}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Fast and slow compression of air in a syringe: adiabatic and isothermal changes
questions.question: Air in a sealed syringe is compressed to half its volume, once very quickly and once very slowly, starting each time from the same pressure \(p_0\) and room temperature. Take \(\gamma=1.4\) for air, and \(2^{1.4}\approx2.64\). Which statement describes the two cases correctly?
options: A) In both cases the pressure becomes \(2p_0\) and the temperature does not change
B) Quick: the pressure becomes \(2p_0\); slow: the pressure becomes \(2.64p_0\)
C) Quick: the pressure becomes about \(2.64p_0\) and the air warms; slow: the pressure becomes \(2p_0\) and the temperature stays the same
D) Quick: the pressure becomes about \(2.64p_0\) and the air cools
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Quick: the pressure becomes about \(2.64p_0\) and the air warms; slow: the pressure becomes \(2p_0\) and the temperature stays the same.
Given: \(V\to\tfrac V2,\quad\gamma=1.4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{isothermal: }pV=\text{const};\quad\text{adiabatic: }pV^\gamma=\text{const},\ TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{const}\)
Step 1: \(\text{slow (isothermal): }p=p_0\cdot2=2p_0\)
Step 2: \(\text{quick (adiabatic): }p=p_0\cdot2^{1.4}\approx2.64p_0\)
Step 3: \(T=T_0\cdot2^{0.4}\approx1.32T_0\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{p_{\text{ad}}}{p_{\text{iso}}}=\frac{2^{1.4}}{2}=2^{0.4}\approx1.32\]
Check: \[\frac{pV}{T}\ \text{for the quick case: }\frac{2.64p_0\cdot\tfrac V2}{1.32T_0}=\frac{p_0V}{T_0}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{work done on the gas in a quick compression cannot leave as heat, so}\ T\ \text{rises}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{true only for the slow case}\); (B) \(\text{swaps the two cases}\); (D) \(\text{work done on a gas with}\ Q=0\ \text{raises}\ U\ \text{and}\ T\).
Key point: \(\text{adiabatic curve is steeper:}\ \dfrac{dp}{dV}=-\gamma\dfrac pV\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Displacement at which kinetic and potential energies are equal in SHM
questions.question: A particle performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude A. At what displacement from the mean position is its kinetic energy equal to its potential energy?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac A{\sqrt2}\).
Given: \(\text{amplitude}\ A,\ \text{total energy}\ E=\tfrac12kA^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(U=\tfrac12kx^2,\quad K=E-U=\tfrac12k(A^2-x^2)\)
Step 1: \(K=U\Rightarrow\tfrac12k(A^2-x^2)=\tfrac12kx^2\)
Step 2: \(A^2=2x^2\)
Worked derivation: \[x=\pm\frac{A}{\sqrt2}\approx\pm0.71A\]
Check: \[U=\tfrac12k\frac{A^2}2=\frac E2,\ K=E-\frac E2=\frac E2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each energy is half of the constant total}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(x=\tfrac A2:\ U=\tfrac E4,\ K=\tfrac{3E}4\); (C) \(U=\tfrac E{16}\); (D) \(U=\tfrac{3E}4,\ K=\tfrac E4\).
Key point: \(U=\dfrac{x^2}{A^2}E\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Standing waves on a string fixed at both ends: nodes and antinodes for a given frequency
questions.question: A string 0.50 m long is fixed at both ends, has a tension of 100 N and a linear mass density of 0.010 kg/m. It is made to vibrate in a standing wave of frequency 300 Hz. How many nodes (counting the two ends) and how many antinodes are there?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4 nodes and 3 antinodes.
Given: \(L=0.50\ \mathrm m,\ T=100\ \mathrm N,\ \mu=0.010\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}},\ f=300\ \mathrm{Hz}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac T\mu};\quad f_n=\dfrac{nv}{2L};\ \text{mode}\ n\ \text{has}\ n\ \text{antinodes and}\ n+1\ \text{nodes}\)
Step 1: \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{100}{0.010}}=100\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(f_1=\dfrac{100}{2\times0.50}=100\ \mathrm{Hz}\Rightarrow n=\dfrac{300}{100}=3\)
Worked derivation: \[\lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{100}{300}=\frac13\ \mathrm m,\quad L=3\cdot\frac\lambda2\Rightarrow\text{3 loops: 3 antinodes, 4 nodes}\]
Check: \[\text{node spacing}=\frac\lambda2=\frac16\ \mathrm m;\ \text{nodes at}\ 0,\tfrac16,\tfrac13,\tfrac12\ \mathrm m\ (4)\]
Why: \(\text{waves reflected at the fixed ends superpose to form loops of length}\ \tfrac\lambda2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{misses one end node}\); (B) \(\text{a string fixed at both ends has one more node than antinodes}\); (D) \(\text{counts only the end nodes}\).
Key point: \(\text{fixed–fixed, mode}\ n:\ n\ \text{antinodes},\ n+1\ \text{nodes}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Field on the axis of a uniformly charged ring: zero at the centre, maximum, and far-field fall-off
questions.question: A thin ring of radius R carries a charge Q spread uniformly. How does the magnitude of the electric field on its axis change as a point moves from the centre of the ring to a very large distance along the axis?
options: A) It is greatest at the centre and falls steadily with distance
B) It is the same everywhere on the axis
C) It is zero at the centre and rises steadily, never decreasing
D) It is zero at the centre, rises to a maximum at a distance \(\tfrac R{\sqrt2}\), and then falls off as \(\tfrac1{x^2}\) far away
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It is zero at the centre, rises to a maximum at a distance \(\tfrac R{\sqrt2}\), and then falls off as \(\tfrac1{x^2}\) far away.
Given: \(\text{ring: radius}\ R,\ \text{charge}\ Q;\ \text{point on axis at distance}\ x\)
Formula/Principle: \(E(x)=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Qx}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}\ \text{(perpendicular components cancel)}\)
Step 1: \(E(0)=0\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dE}{dx}\propto\dfrac{(R^2+x^2)-3x^2}{(R^2+x^2)^{5/2}}=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac R{\sqrt2}\)
Step 3: \(x\gg R:\ E\approx\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{x^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[E_{\max}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q\,R/\sqrt2}{(3R^2/2)^{3/2}}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{2Q}{3\sqrt3R^2}\]
Check: \[x=R:\ E=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{2\sqrt2R^2}=\frac{0.354Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0R^2}<E_{\max}=\frac{0.385Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0R^2}\]
Why: \(\text{at the centre, fields from opposite elements cancel; far away the ring looks like a point charge}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(E(0)=0\ \text{by symmetry}\); (B) \(E\ \text{depends on}\ x\); (C) \(E\to0\ \text{as}\ x\to\infty\).
Key point: \(E_{\text{axis}}=\dfrac{kQx}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}},\ \text{maximum at}\ x=\tfrac R{\sqrt2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Reading field strength and direction from unequally spaced equipotential lines; path-independent work
questions.question: The figure shows four equipotential lines in a region of electric field, with their potentials and positions marked on the x-axis. A charge \(q=+2.0\ \mu\mathrm C\) is moved from point P on the 40 V line to point Q on the 10 V line along the curved dashed path. Which statement is correct?
options: A) The field is strongest near the 10 V line, and the field does \(-60\ \mu\mathrm J\) of work on the charge
B) The field is strongest between the 40 V and 30 V lines (about 1000 V/m), points towards lower potential, and does \(+60\ \mu\mathrm J\) of work on the charge whatever the path
C) The field is the same everywhere, 500 V/m, and the work depends on the path taken
D) The field is strongest between the 20 V and 10 V lines because the lines are farthest apart there, and the field does \(+60\ \mu\mathrm J\) of work
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The field is strongest between the 40 V and 30 V lines (about 1000 V/m), points towards lower potential, and does \(+60\ \mu\mathrm J\) of work on the charge whatever the path.
Given: \(\text{from the figure: }V=40,30,20,10\ \mathrm V\ \text{at}\ x=0,1,3,6\ \mathrm{cm};\ q=2.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm C\)
Formula/Principle: \(E=-\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta x}\ \text{(perpendicular to equipotentials)};\quad W_{\text{field}}=q(V_P-V_Q)\)
Step 1: \(E_{40\to30}=\dfrac{10\ \mathrm V}{0.01\ \mathrm m}=1000\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(E_{30\to20}=\dfrac{10}{0.02}=500\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}},\quad E_{20\to10}=\dfrac{10}{0.03}\approx333\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\)
Step 3: \(W=2.0\times10^{-6}\,(40-10)=6.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm J=60\ \mu\mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[E\ \text{points along}\ +x\ (\text{from 40 V towards 10 V});\quad W_{\text{field}}=q\Delta V_{\text{drop}}=+60\ \mu\mathrm J\]
Check: \[\Delta U=q(V_Q-V_P)=-60\ \mu\mathrm J=-W_{\text{field}}\ \checkmark;\ \text{a positive charge loses energy moving to lower}\ V\]
Why: \(\text{closer equipotentials mean a larger potential gradient; the electrostatic field is conservative}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{lines are farthest apart near 10 V, so}\ E\ \text{is weakest there; the work is positive}\); (C) \(\text{the spacing is not uniform, and electrostatic work is path-independent}\); (D) \(\text{wider spacing means a weaker field}\).
Key point: \(E=\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta x}\ \text{is largest where equipotentials crowd together}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Field of a solenoid measured with a Hall probe: changing turn density and current; field at an end
questions.question: A Hall probe at the centre of a long solenoid (500 turns, length 0.50 m) carrying 2.0 A reads 2.5 mT. The same solenoid is then stretched uniformly to a length of 1.0 m, still with 500 turns, and the current is raised to 3.0 A. It is still long compared with its radius. About what will the probe read at the centre, and about what at one end on the axis?
options: A) 1.9 mT at the centre and 0.94 mT at an end
B) 3.8 mT at the centre and 1.9 mT at an end
C) 1.9 mT at the centre and 1.9 mT at an end
D) 0.94 mT at the centre and 1.9 mT at an end
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1.9 mT at the centre and 0.94 mT at an end.
Given: \(n_1=\dfrac{500}{0.50}=1000\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},\ I_1=2.0\ \mathrm A,\ B_1=2.5\ \mathrm{mT};\quad n_2=\dfrac{500}{1.0}=500\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},\ I_2=3.0\ \mathrm A\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Ampere's law: }B_{\text{centre}}=\mu_0nI;\quad B_{\text{end}}\approx\tfrac12\mu_0nI\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{B_2}{B_1}=\dfrac{n_2I_2}{n_1I_1}=\dfrac{500\times3.0}{1000\times2.0}=0.75\)
Step 2: \(B_2=0.75\times2.5=1.875\ \mathrm{mT}\approx1.9\ \mathrm{mT}\)
Step 3: \(B_{\text{end}}\approx\dfrac{1.875}2\approx0.94\ \mathrm{mT}\)
Worked derivation: \[B_2=\mu_0n_2I_2=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times500\times3.0=1.88\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm T\]
Check: \[B_1=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times1000\times2.0=2.51\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm T\approx2.5\ \mathrm{mT}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at an end, only the turns on one side contribute, giving half the central field}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{keeps}\ n=1000\ \mathrm{m^{-1}};\ \text{stretching halves}\ n\); (C) \(\text{the field is not uniform up to the ends}\); (D) \(\text{swaps centre and end}\).
Key point: \(B=\mu_0nI\ \text{depends on turns per unit length, not total turns}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Magnet falling through a copper tube and a plastic tube: Lenz's law
questions.question: Identical strong magnets are dropped from rest through two vertical tubes of the same length and size, one made of copper and one of plastic. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Both magnets take the same time, because no current is connected to either tube
B) The magnet in the copper tube falls faster, because copper attracts the magnet
C) The magnet in the plastic tube falls more slowly, because plastic is an insulator and stores charge
D) The magnet in the copper tube takes longer, because the changing flux induces currents in the copper whose magnetic field opposes the magnet's motion
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The magnet in the copper tube takes longer, because the changing flux induces currents in the copper whose magnetic field opposes the magnet's motion.
Given: \(\text{copper: conductor};\ \text{plastic: insulator};\ \text{same magnets and tubes}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\varepsilon=-\dfrac{d\Phi_B}{dt}\ \text{(Faraday)};\ \text{induced current opposes the change (Lenz)}\)
Step 1: \(\text{copper: changing}\ \Phi_B\ \text{through each ring of the tube}\Rightarrow\text{eddy currents}\)
Step 2: \(\text{these currents give a field that repels the magnet from above and attracts it from below}\Rightarrow\text{retarding force}\ F\propto v\)
Step 3: \(\text{plastic: no free charges, no currents}\Rightarrow a=g\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{copper: }mg-bv=ma\Rightarrow v\to v_t=\frac{mg}b;\qquad\text{plastic: }t=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{g}}\]
Check: \[\text{energy: copper tube warms up; mechanical energy is turned into heat, so the magnet arrives slower and later}\]
Why: \(\text{Lenz's law is energy conservation for induced currents}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{induced currents need no external source}\); (B) \(\text{copper is not attracted by a static magnet; the force opposes motion}\); (C) \(\text{no currents in plastic, so no opposing force}\).
Key point: \(\text{induced currents oppose the motion that causes them}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Peak current of an AC heater and the equivalent DC voltage for the same power
questions.question: A heater (pure resistor) dissipates 1100 W when connected to a 220 V rms AC supply. What is the peak current through it, and what steady DC voltage would make it dissipate the same power?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 7.1 A and 220 V.
Given: \(P=1100\ \mathrm W,\quad V_{\text{rms}}=220\ \mathrm V\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}};\quad I_0=\sqrt2I_{\text{rms}};\quad\text{rms value}=\text{DC value giving the same heating}\)
Step 1: \(I_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{1100}{220}=5.0\ \mathrm A\)
Step 2: \(I_0=\sqrt2\times5.0=7.07\ \mathrm A\approx7.1\ \mathrm A\)
Worked derivation: \[R=\frac{V_{\text{rms}}^2}{P}=\frac{48400}{1100}=44\ \Omega;\qquad V_{\text{DC}}=\sqrt{PR}=\sqrt{1100\times44}=220\ \mathrm V\]
Check: \[\langle i^2\rangle R=\frac{I_0^2}{2}R=\frac{50}{2}\times44=1100\ \mathrm W\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{average power in a resistor depends on}\ \langle i^2\rangle=\tfrac{I_0^2}2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(5.0\ \mathrm A\ \text{is the rms current; 311 V is the peak voltage}\); (C) \(\text{a DC of 311 V would give}\ \tfrac{311^2}{44}\approx2200\ \mathrm W\); (D) \(5.0\ \mathrm A\ \text{is rms, not peak}\).
Key point: \(I_0=\sqrt2I_{\text{rms}};\ \text{equal heating}\iff V_{\text{DC}}=V_{\text{rms}}\)

questions.sub_topic: Reading the critical angle from a graph of refraction angle against incidence angle
questions.question: Light passes from medium A into medium B. The figure shows the angle of refraction r in B plotted against the angle of incidence i in A; no refracted ray is observed for incidence angles beyond the end of the curve. Take \(\sin42^\circ=0.67\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(\dfrac{n_A}{n_B}=0.67\), and at \(i=50^\circ\) the ray emerges along the surface
B) \(\dfrac{n_A}{n_B}\approx1.5\), and at \(i=50^\circ\) the ray is refracted at about \(70^\circ\)
C) \(\dfrac{n_A}{n_B}\approx1.5\), and at \(i=50^\circ\) all the light is reflected back into A
D) \(\dfrac{n_B}{n_A}\approx1.5\), and at \(i=50^\circ\) all the light is reflected back into A
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{n_A}{n_B}\approx1.5\), and at \(i=50^\circ\) all the light is reflected back into A.
Given: \(\text{from the figure: }r=90^\circ\ \text{at}\ i=i_c=42^\circ;\ \sin42^\circ=0.67\)
Formula/Principle: \(n_A\sin i=n_B\sin r;\quad\text{critical angle: }\sin i_c=\dfrac{n_B}{n_A}\)
Step 1: \(r>i\ \text{on the curve}\Rightarrow\text{B is optically rarer}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{n_B}{n_A}=\sin42^\circ=0.67\Rightarrow\dfrac{n_A}{n_B}=\dfrac1{0.67}\approx1.5\)
Step 3: \(i=50^\circ>i_c\Rightarrow\sin r=1.5\sin50^\circ=1.5\times0.766=1.15>1\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{n_A}{n_B}=\frac{1}{\sin i_c}=\frac1{0.67}=1.49\approx1.5;\qquad i>i_c\Rightarrow\text{total internal reflection}\]
Check: \[i=30^\circ:\ \sin r=1.49\times0.5=0.75\Rightarrow r\approx48^\circ>30^\circ,\ \text{consistent with the curve lying above}\ r=i\]
Why: \(\text{the curve ends at}\ r=90^\circ;\ \text{beyond}\ i_c\ \text{no real}\ r\ \text{exists}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(0.67\ \text{is}\ \tfrac{n_B}{n_A}\); (B) \(\sin r=1.15>1\ \text{is impossible}\); (D) \(\text{if}\ n_B>n_A,\ r<i\ \text{and there is no critical angle}\).
Key point: \(\sin i_c=\dfrac{n_{\text{rarer}}}{n_{\text{denser}}}\)
